Description: This bar offers pinchos and tapas, or Spanish cuisine served on small plates. A casual place to enjoy Basque home cooking along with drinks from Spain. The Basque Country is rich with the blessings of mountains and sea, so the range of offerings covers a wide gamut. Each item is simple, the portions generous. Though a continent apart, Spain and Japan share a love of honest cooking in which natural flavours come to the fore.

Name: Akihana
Description: To revisit the basics after studying creative Chinese cooking, the chef adds polish to a selection of Chinese regional cuisines. Sichuan items dominate, including steamed chicken with spicy sauce, twice-cooked pork and shrimp in chili sauce. The signature mapo tofu is a true original, made with wagyu beef sinew instead of ground meat. Faithful to his Shizuoka roots, he prepares his XO sauce fried rice with stardust shrimps and dried fish fry to create a mutual understanding between the cuisines of Kyoto and the Suruga region.

Name: Ramen Touhichi
Description: Ramen that’s all about the goodness of chicken, imparting its flavour in purest form. Ramen Touhichi’s signature soy-sauce ramen uses dashi made only with locally raised free-range chicken and water, mixing it with raw soy sauce kaeshi. Other offerings include richly flavoursome chicken boiled in plain water, cold noodles soaked in kombu dashi soup served with dipping sauce of chicken soy sauce, and chicken-oil noodles served without soup. ‘Touhichi’ is named after the house where the chef was born. See him at the counter full of pride in his native Kyoto.

Name: Chinese Noodles ROKU
Address: 2F, Good Nature Station, 318-6 Inaricho, Shimogyo-ku, Kyoto, 600-8022, Japan
Description: Ramen, soup and other Chinese foods are the soul of this ramen shop by Velrosier. The chef draws soup stock from bones of duck, chicken, venison and pork. Clear soup owes its depth to umami from a medley of dried foods; dried longan fruit, a Chinese medicinal herb, is a touch only a gourmet of Chinese cuisine would think of. The manifold layers of flavour derive from Roku’s ‘add-on’ approach to seasoning.

Name: Ramen Kuon
Address: B2F, Semba Centar Bldg Sangokan, 1-4-3 Sembachuo, Chuo-ku, Osaka, 541-0055, Japan
Description: The chef takes pride in his “Shio Soba” (salt noodles), his quest for a bowl of perfection. Taste the seaweed—sea lettuce and nori—and you can feel the rustle of sea breezes. Triple soup of fish, shellfish and chicken is prepared using Pi-Water, a water that is said to be extremely similar to water in living tissue. High hydration ramen noodles, prepared with a blend of three types of wheat flour, produces a texture similar to noodles kneaded by hand. Three types of chashu are served as well, combining pork and chicken. Bringing out the best in soup, noodles and chashu for a triple treat.

Name: Osteria La Cicerchia
Description: The ‘Marches cuisine specialty restaurant’ certificate from Italy proudly adorns the wall, and indeed the gastronomy of this region on Italy’s Adriatic coast is what the chef excels in. Meat-stuffed olive fritti, homemade salsiccia and rabbit-and-tomato stew are all staples of the Marchese dining board. Cicerchia beans are a classic legume grown in the town where the chef stayed. Their flavour can be tasted in her minestrone soup.

Name: Sobakiri Gaku
Description: It’s counter seating only in this modern interior accented with natural materials. The chef likes his soba to have a certain translucency, so he kneads it into ni-hachi, which contains 20% wheat flour. Soba is served cold on wicker baskets, not in soup, so patrons can appreciate the fragrance and firmness of the grain. ‘Kaeshi’, a mixture of soy sauce, sugar and mirin, is used to good effect in the rich dipping sauce, displaying the chef’s Kanto training. ‘Gaku’ means ‘mountain and sky’, signifying the chef’s commitment to attain ever higher goals.

Name: Ramen Hayato
Description: This long-serving ramen shop is loved by Japanese people for its “Three Great Ramens”: soy-sauce, salt and miso. First-time visitors are recommended to order the soy-sauce ramen, but once you learn that the Hokkaido-born chef studied in Sapporo, you might be tempted to go for the miso ramen. The soy-sauce ramen is served in a double soup of meat-based stock and seafood-based stock. “Ura-Shoyu”, the ‘hidden soy-sauce ramen’ not listed on the menu, uses meat-based stock only. If you’re having trouble deciding, start with the ‘official’ menu.

Name: Sobakiri Karani
Description: Sobakiri Karani worked with a woodworking artist to create the interior using re-used wooden materials. Large tables with mismatched chairs and unique ceiling paintings express a whimsical spirit. The menu’s appetisers, including tofu pickled in unrefined sake and duck-and-onion miso, tempts one to a cup of sake. Soba is coarse-ground and cut into both thin and thick noodles, furnishing variety in finish and flavours. Enjoy soba the way you like it in a congenial atmosphere.

Name: Berangkat
Description: Berangkat means ‘beginnings’ in Indonesian, apt for a restaurant serving creative interpretations of cuisine the owner-chef studied in Southeast Asia. Consider, for example, shiraae dressed with coriander, pidan and Szechuan pickles, drizzled with homemade chilli oil. The grilled meat in cinnamon soy sauce borrows from the fare of the street stalls of Vietnam. The Okinawa cuisine, from the owner-chef’s experiences on Ishigakijima Island, is another of the restaurant’s fortes.

Name: Ishii Jr.
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Shoes must be removed
Description: Manning the grill at this yakitori shop, sister of Torisho Ishii, is the apprentice of Yoshitomo Ishii, the original shop’s owner-chef. Both the assembly of the skewers and the way they are grilled reflect Ishii’s tutelage, as does the practice of using chicken from different regions, primarily Kumamoto, Wakayama and Akita prefectures. The line-up ranges from perennial yakitori favourites to more unusual cuts such as chochin (chicken yolk sac) and chicken testes.

Name: Macauda
Description: Tuna tartare; simmered squid in ink; mackerel meunière- the large number of fish dishes derives from the chef’s apprenticeship days. Working in the southern Italian regions of Puglia and Sicily, he was struck by the similarity of its food culture with Japan’s, with its emphasis on seafood. The chef respects the region’s techniques while incorporating ingredients in season. Always on the lookout for opportunities to hone his skills, he spends evenings focusing on hand-made pasta.

Name: Asperge Blanche
Description: White is the keynote colour of the antiques-accented interior. The restaurant is decorated with sundries collected at flea markets, while a pendant light wreathes the establishment in its warm glow. The chef prepares traditional cuisine, arrangements stripped to the essentials so the flavours of the ingredients themselves shine clearly. Enamoured of Bincho charcoal, the chef even bakes his bread with it. The name of the restaurant means ‘white asparagus’—no need to ask what their spring speciality is…

Name: KOBUSHI Ramen
Description: The owner-chef created his menu by trial and error, driven by the search for ingredients that are quintessentially Kyoto. Turning his eye to locally raised duck, he conceived his renowned ‘Kyoto Duck and Dried Nodoguro Soba’. The soup is prepared with dashi of duck bones and tai heads and enriched with dashi of venison bones; the garnish of Kujo green onions is a consummate Kyoto touch. Those who lean toward lighter flavours should try the ‘Rausu kombu Kake Soba’.

Name: Sumiyakisosaitoriya Hitomi
Description: Sumiyakisosaitoriya Hitomi is full night after night and the delicious grilled chicken is only one reason for this success. The other is the character of the owner-chef. He stays in guests’ line of sight at all times as he assiduously works the Kishu-binchotan charcoal. He guides his service staff of students with fatherly kindness and makes guests feel like family. The restaurant offers baby chicken, local chicken and brand-name chicken, for their differences in taste and texture. Enjoy devotion and passion in every skewer.

Name: Tonkatsu Daiki
Description: ‘Daiki’ was the full name when the owner-chef’s parents ran it as a teishoku restaurant. The second-generation owner-chef switched to specialising in tonkatsu. Pork from Kagoshima is deep-fried in salad oil to provide the batter with just the right crispness. His experience in Chinese cooking comes to the fore in the piquantly spiced mustard sauce He pays special attention to the rice, too, cooking it in small batches.

Name: BOCCA del VINO
Description: The quirky name, ‘mouth of wine’, reflects the chef’s fond memories of Italy, where jugs of wine graced every dinner table. The chef studied in the southern Italy, so recipes are simple, prepared with lashings of tomatoes and olive oil. Seafood features prominently in appetisers, meat and poultry in main dishes, based on the chef’s experiences. Pasta is dressed with the familiar oil, tomatoes and ragu. Comfort food that brings to mind daily life in Italy.

Name: au soleil couchant
Description: The French tricolour flies over the district of Yuhigaoka. ‘Au soleil couchant’ means ‘at the setting sun’, a homage to this couple’s apprenticeship in Lyon and to Yuhigaoka, which means ‘hill of the setting sun’. The chef as culinary artisan commands the kitchen, while his pâtissière wife serves customers. As in any good bistro, portions are generous. Pleasingly, vegetables are used in abundance. Respect for tradition and true French spirit permeate the establishment.

Name: Az
Description: Billing itself as a ‘Chinese bistro’, Az serves Chinese fare with wine from an assortment of countries. The menu is resplendent with local colour. If stir-fry of wagyu beef is for you, you can choose your sauce from among Guangdong-style oyster sauce, Sichuan-style yúxiāng and Beijing-style miso. Pairing sweet, sour and spicy flavours with a suitable wine provides an added dimension of fun. At lunch, under the name Bifun Azuma, the restaurant serves fried rice vermicelli (‘bifun’ in Japanese) and Chinese zongzi.

Name: Soba Rojina
Description: To convey the unique character of the soba, the owner-chef prepares juwari with no wheat flour. He made the stone mortar he uses to grind the flour himself, back when he was an apprentice. The entire shop reverberates with the sound of buckwheat being ground slowly so as to retain the fragrance. In addition to soba, Rojina offers items that pair well with alcohol. Tofu with yuba on top and manganji togarashi with jako are two typical Kyoto appetisers served before the soba.

Name: Udondokoro Shigemi
Description: The chef’s top recommendation is the ‘hiyakake’: nothing but udon noodles in a golden-yellow broth. The dashi is Kansai-style, made with makombu seaweed for umami and finely chopped round herring and mackerel for flavour. Noodles are prepared with techniques learned in Kagawa. The cool broth brings out the supple body and elasticity of the noodles, showing how the goodness of each supports the other. The donburi bowl here brings together the udon cultures of Osaka and Kagawa.

Name: Soba Takama
Description: ‘Mori soba’ means ‘soba piled high’, and it is. Soba is served on seiro (bamboo or wicker baskets) because in the days of the Tokugawa shoguns it was common to steam the noodles. Piling soba into a mountain is another practice rooted in history. Made from buckwheat grains stripped of their black husks, this mori soba has a delicious finish. Inaka soba, made from husked whole buckwheat grains, is gloriously fragrant. Dipping sauce brightened with kombu kelp reflects the dashi stock culture of the Kansai region. We love the generous portions—one plate fully satisfies.

Name: Gombei
Description: Fans of Gombei think immediately of udon or soba with kitsune (deep-fried tofu), but certainly not with tanuki (deep-fried tempura pieces). The menu begins with udon, showing how popular it is. Two types of kitsune are available, one with chopped tofu, the other with tofu simmered in sweetened soy sauce. ‘Keiran’ is a warm udon dish topped with a starch sauce of soft scrambled eggs and ginger. Noodles are boiled soft to soak up the dashi. A taste of Kyoto, beloved of kabuki actors, geisha and maiko.

Name: Gion Yorozuya
Description: When Gion Yorozuya was founded, its focus was on meal deliveries to teahouses and playhouses. The restaurant thrived thanks to a favourable reception from geisha and maiko, and today guests queue up at the door well before opening time. The dish of renown is the onion udon. Eager to use Kyoto foodstuffs, the chef smothers his plates in Kujo spring onion. The three pillars of the cuisine that keeps customers coming back are tender noodles, dashi and onions. “Mari”, a dish larded with pickled plums, and “Tsunoda”, enhanced with chicken meat, are named for the celebrities who favour these ingredients.

Name: Hiiragitei
Description: It’s a family affair at this restaurant specialising in locally raised chicken and obanzai: the father prepares the à la carte dishes, the son the yakitori, and the mother attends to customers’ needs. Every morning the son visits a poultry farm in Shiga Prefecture to purchase and dress whole chickens by himself. The speciality of the house is the white liver, a rare part of the chicken, and back liver complemented with the bitter flavour of cacao nibs.

Name: Sakeya Sakana Yoshimura
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Cash only,Counter dining,Notable sake list
Description: This kappo izakaya is run by a sake-loving couple. The husband tends the kitchen, the wife warms the sake. The menu, crafted to double as bar snacks, is dominated by seafood. Jellied conger eel broth, vegetables seasoned with vinegar and miso and freshly deep-fried tofu are standard fare. Attention is paid to details: seaweed is toasted over charcoal, dried bonito shaved just before serving. The intimate pub seats three guests at the most; on certain days, it’s exclusively for a single tippler.

Name: Benikurage
Description: The owner-chef and his wife tour sake breweries throughout Japan to select their favourites. Not surprisingly, the cuisine is oriented towards how it pairs with sake. The fish for sashimi is aged to enhance flavour. Clear broth soup is a constant companion, as they believe in the match between sake and kombu kelp. Sagohachi pickled lamb is flavoured with rice malt, pairing nicely with sake. The name means ‘immortal jellyfish’, after a creature whose cells regenerate so it never gets old. Similarly, the couple’s passion for cuisine and sake never fades.

Name: Washoku Haru
Description: The blackboard menu is inscribed with familiar Japanese comfort foods such as braised and seasoned burdock root, sukiyaki and fried minced meat cake. Potato salad is not mashed but entwined with cream; steamed wheat-gluten, wrapped in seaweed and fried, is pleasingly buttery; and mackerel sushi is served rolled and wrapped in seaweed. The owner-chef fine-tunes his dishes, making every dish fascinating. Oden stew is a fun treat in winter, thanks to his experience in the art of simmering. Stir-fried noodles and ramen are tempting choices as well.

Name: HUNTER
Description: Chef Imai is as obsessed with meat as a hunter stalking his game. Putting his experience with French cuisine to work, he grills his meat-centric menu on a charcoal grill. In addition to duck, pork and beef, in autumn and winter Imai serves game meats such as boar and deer. Charcuterie such as pâté and rillettes are arranged on plates that look like stumps for a natural look. If you sit at the counter, you’ll have the pleasure of chatting with this personable chef.

Name: ricuperare TAKEUCHI
Description: Wood, charcoal and straw all fuel the cooking flames at this trattoria. The aim is to find the perfect flame for each ingredient. Beef is grilled over a wood fire for its moisture, a charcoal fire for its heat; for duck and bonito, straw is burned for its fragrance. True to its name, which means ‘recover’, the restaurant wastes nothing, using meat and vegetable ends to make breads and sauces. It also means to restore guests in both health and spirit.

Name: Oito
Description: The building, in the style of a townhouse, stands on Kiritoshi Alley in Gion. Portraits of maiko adorn the walls, reinforcing the geisha-district ambience. ‘Lunch Oden’ is the only item on the menu. The owner-chef is mindful of retaining familiar and comforting flavours. Lunch consists of five items of the diner’s choice, accompanied by takikomi-gohan. The choice of oden is up to the customer, but if you choose the popular beef tendon, we recommend pairing it with the tofu or konnyaku.

Name: KORISU
Description: A mother and two daughters, in their pure-white smocks, make guests feel at home with their family hospitality. French and other Western dishes are served with generous portions, bringing satisfaction that keeps the restaurant’s reputation strong. Hamburger steak and fried shrimp are flavours from the good old days. Escargot and lamb pair well with wine. With only three tables, and the phone often unanswered, getting a reservation can be a bit of a scramble.

Name: Bistro des Chenapans
Description: The chef of this bistro takes pride in his meat cuisine, having studied meat processing in Paris. Casual prix fixe menus of hamburger steak and the like are popular at lunchtime. In the evening, guests can dine à la carte from the charcuterie, cassoulet and so forth. In a bow to the chef’s roots in Shiga Prefecture, Omi beef is used in the steak and fries. Meat is drizzled in oil as it grills to bring out its aroma, and seasoned simply with salt and pepper.

Name: Hommachi Seimenjo Chukasobakobo
Address: B2F, Semba Centar Bldg Nigokan, 1-3-2 Sembachuo, Chuo-ku, Osaka, 541-0055, Japan
Description: When you visit this ramen shop launched by a dried foods wholesaler, take note of the soup, which epitomises the brilliance of the dashi soup stock. Its well-rounded fragrance derives from multiple types of dried fish flakes. Kombu kelp, pike conger and chicken bones each add layers of flavour, creating body and finish. Heightening the taste are two types of noodles made on the premises: flat noodles to soak up the soup, round ones for their texture.

Name: Shokudo Akari
Description: Akari shines out of a detached house in the entertainment district. The nest of criss-crossing wooden poles hung from the ceiling represent the handheld pine torches of the Oto Fire Festival in Wakayama, as well as the flame of the chef’s passion for cooking. Expect everything from familiar favourites such as gingered chicken liver, potato salad and deep-fried horse mackerel, to seasonal flavours. Naturally, this true son of Wakayama takes pride in grilling with Kishu Bincho charcoal. Every February 6, the chef returns to his native prefecture to take part in the Fire Festival.

Name: Ayamedo
Description: The building used to be a merchant house and now sports a Showa-era vibe. Side dishes such as tofu preserved in miso, buckwheat dumplings and bowls of duck meat fill the menu to accompany drinks. Not a few guests can be seen tipping a cup or two from noon onwards in the retro atmosphere. The soba noodles are generously piled high like a mountain on a wicker draining basket, dazzling the eyes, and each noodle, with its sharp, angular shape, offers a firm yet smooth texture.

Name: Sobashubo Ichii
Description: The marquee dishes here are hand-made soba and duck preparations. Seiro makes sparing use of filler to bring out the suppleness and flavour of the noodles. Osaka Kawachi ducks are used, a good fit for the dipping sauce thanks to their tender flesh and sweet fat. When you savour the kamo nanban or duck seiro, you can taste the affinity between soba and duck. In the evening, imaginative duck creations are on offer, not to mention soba sushi of chicken breast and daikon radish, or Japanese ajillo of gizzard and mushrooms.

Name: il luogo di TAKEUCHI
Description: This is the main branch of Takeuchi, which operates a number of casual Italian trattorias. The owner-chef holds court in the kitchen, directing his cooking staff. At noontime a simple pasta lunch is served, but a full range of à la carte dishes are offered in the evening. The range of pastas is impressive, and the eatery does not skimp on tomato and cream sauces. The aroma of fish and wagyu grilling over charcoal is also compelling.

Name: Menya Inoichi
Description: From the front of the restaurant comes the tempting aroma of dashi, inviting the diner in. True to their Kyoto roots, they pursue a ramen richly suffused with the flavour of dashi. The broth is from Rausu kombu, a type of kelp rich in umami, and several types of dried seafood. The feature dish is ‘Dashi Soba’. The ramen is served in two varieties: the lightly seasoned ‘white’ and the full-bodied ‘black.’ Freshly shaved katsuo-bushi brings out the umami still further.

Name: Taiho
Description: This Chinese restaurant is run by a family, who all support each other. The father’s offerings, which have pleased the locals for generations, sit side-by-side with authentic Szechuan cuisine from the son’s gastronomic studies. One dish for which Taiho has been renowned since its opening is the ‘Teridon Kinshi’. This quintessentially Kyoto dish consists of rice topped with pork and kinshi tamago (ribbons of omelette). Also recommended is the ‘Yodaredori’, steamed chicken with a spicy sauce.

Name: Muromachi Kaji
Description: This kappo izakaya heaves with customers night after night. Sashimi combinations are arranged as for kaiseki traditional multi-course meals. The inclusion of chub mackerel sushi is gratifying. Potatoes are paired with delicacies to conjure a potato salad for grownups that goes well with sake. Plovers emblazoned on the shop curtain and towels are for good luck, representing the overcoming of rough seas. The staff work as a tight-knit crew to surmount the waves of orders the shop’s popularity brings them.

Name: KASHIWAI
Description: Founded as an antique store, the shop is still decorated with old pottery. ‘Temarizushi’, little sushi balls served in thin cardboard boxes, are as cute as wagashi confections. Seafood and vegetables for sushi are crafted with great care as well. Sea bream is marinated in kombu, shiitake mushrooms are simmered slowly in dashi. Kyoto food culture is woven into the entire menu, as shown by simmered bamboo shoots served in spring and pickled sliced radishes called ‘senmaizuke’ offered in winter. The restaurant is open from morning onwards; for dinner seating, reservations are required.

Name: Aozora blue
Description: This distinctive udon is prepared using the techniques of handmade soba, which the chef mastered before switching to udon. Unpolished wheat is ground on a millstone. The experience of the soba craftsman lives in the principle of ‘freshly ground, freshly rolled, freshly boiled’. We recommend the Arabiki Zaru Udon (coarse-ground udon served on a wicker basket). Salt and wasabi accompany the dish, and the meal ends with udon water (not soba water, as is the practice elsewhere). Alcoholic drinks and snacks are selected to befit an udon meal. The chef’s discovery of wheat changed his life; the paths of both soba and udon are long and narrow.

Name: Choshoku Kishin
Description: Breakfast is the only meal served here; rice dishes with soup. Rice is served from the first plume of steam, before it is fully cooked. Choshoku Kishin weaves together the format of tea ceremony cuisine. Guests choose a rice bowl, then select from an assortment of soups. Rice is doled out little by little, so you can experience the change in flavour as steaming progresses. Accompaniments include whole dried round herring and pickled veg. This is the spot for a delightful breakfast with gracious service. Reservations required.

Name: Bistro Yanagihara
Description: A bistro by a chef who apprenticed in Alsace. For appetisers, he showcases his skills with choucroute of salt-pickled fermented cabbage, confit of foie gras and charcuterie of ham and sausages. His main dishes are prepared with no less care: items such as beef simmered in red wine and pâté grilled in a pastry shell have their flavours drawn out over time. Hearty portions ensure a full stomach.

Name: Chukasoba Mugen
Description: While eating ramen, salt water from the noodles gradually dilutes the soup. You can experience this for yourself. First, pour a little of the soup into a separate bowl. Finish the noodles in the original bowl, then try sipping the reserved soup—the difference in taste will amaze you. The harmony created by a bowl of ramen goes beyond taste. The slurping of noodles forms a duet with the classical music in the background. The joy of ramen knows no bounds: ‘mugen’.

Name: Sobakiri Arabompu
Description: ‘Arabompu’ was a favourite word of Edo-era haiku poet Kobayashi Issa. It means ‘living a free and ordinary life’. For the chef here, it means approaching his subjects, buckwheat and soba, from a natural stance. To watch his series of tasks—parboiling, washing, then plating the soba noodles—there’s no substitute for a seat at the counter. The ‘Soba Zanmai’ set offers three types of soba—nihachi, juwari, and arabiki—served as half bowls of each for tasting. Kanto-style dipping sauce recalls the days of the chef’s apprenticeship.

Name: Sobakiri Imose
Description: ‘Imose’ refers to Mt. Imose in Wakayama Prefecture in the Manyoshu. The owner-chef chose it in tribute to his birthplace. This charming space with its sunken hearth recalls the rural scenes of his youth. Eager for customers to taste the differences in texture and aroma of soba types, he produces it in the nihachi, inaka and juwari styles. The kakinohazushi, sushi of shimesaba wrapped in a persimmon leaf, is hometown cooking in Wakayama ; order it with soba for a diverting pairing.

Name: Naniwa Okina
Description: The third-generation owner-chef decided to switch from machine-rolled to hand-rolled soba, so he learned the technique from a master. After thoroughly straining the soba, but without over-cooling it, he cuts the noodles neither thin nor thick, but just right. Dipping sauce is medium-salty to bring out the aroma of the buckwheat seeds, and the dish is arranged beautifully. A full range of snacks are on offer. We hope Japan will always have soba shops like this one.

Name: Kanesho
Description: The shop was founded at the end of the Edo period as a wholesaler of river fish. Situated at the end of an alley as long and narrow as an eel’s bed, Kanesho is recognisable by the leaping eel emblazoned on its noren. ‘Kinshi-don’, the brainchild of the fourth-generation chef, is renowned. This popular dish incorporates ‘kinshitamago’, omelette cut into thin strips, an essential component of Kyoto favourites such as chirashizushi and steamed sushi. ‘Ochazuke Eel’ is eel simmered in dipping sauce and drenched in green tea, a refreshing flavour. A place where one hopes to gain the vitality of the leaping eel.

Name: Shigetsu
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Shoes must be removed
Description: Shojin ryori is a vegetarian cuisine in the Buddhist monastic tradition. It is a part of Buddhist ascetic practice, said to cleanse the soul, suppress worldly desires and promote spiritual growth. It is said that pouring one’s heart into one’s cooking is the secret to true shojin ryori and an act that expresses gratitude for all people. Shojin ryori is a quest not for physical results but for an inner spiritual calm. A guide on the path of life.

Name: Ikkon Uehara
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Shoes must be removed
Description: At lunchtime, only omakase set menus are offered; in the evening, à la carte dishes are also served. Ikkon Uehara aims to cater to a regular clientele, so the menu is comprehensive and the cuisine lovingly prepared. An assorted platter loaded with appetisers show that the old ways are not forgotten. A wooden bowl of fishcake steeped in a clear broth is classic comfort food. The counter is a horigotatsu; behind the counter, the couple in charge deliver cheerful and gracious service. Tip a cup or two of sake and feel the seasons change.

Name: La bonne tâche
Description: Red bell-pepper mousse, smoked salmon, roast duck; ever since it opened, the fare here has been simple, out of respect for the ingredients. The chef seeks to draw closer to perfection every day, advancing in his craft. Cooking skill, recipes and spirituality are all things he learned as an apprentice. Cast your eye around the kitchen and notice how all the pots and pans are gleaming. Respect for the tools of his trade drive the chef to keep honing his technique.

Name: tanpopo
Description: The chef has continually upped his culinary game through a quarter-century of self-instruction, hopping from restaurant to restaurant to sharpen his instincts. The result is his cooking with iron and copper plates. Fluffy omelettes and deep-fried knots of fish paste are grilled on copper, pungent stir-fried noodles and beef steaks on iron. Tonpeiyaki (cabbage and pork wrapped in an omelette) is braced with sage for a hint of Italian. Rum is added to crêpes in the French style. Imagination and passion are cooked into every dish.

Name: Jukuseibuta Kawamura
Description: The nation’s finest pork brands cascade across the menu, so you can choose the type and grade of pork that suits you best. The best is the ‘jukusei-buta’ aged pork that gives the shop its name. Sourced from a butcher in Fushimi, the pork this restaurant handles is rested to enhance its flavour. The plaque on the wall says, ‘Timing is everything’; the pork is deep-fried twice in low-temperature oil, the cooking time expertly judged. Pork katsu curry, seasoned with ginger and spices, is also tempting.

Name: Kyogoku Kaneyo
Description: This eel restaurant has been in business for seven generations, dating back to the Meiji period. Every day finds the shop crowded with customers, many seeking its signature dish of ‘Kinshi Don’: rice covered in dipping sauce and topped with Edo-style eel and a large Kyoto-style omelette. What makes this east-west marriage of flavours work so well is the dipping sauce, a staple since the restaurant’s inception. The Kanto-style kabayaki, which involves steaming eel before grilling and dipping it in sauce, is a technique from a cook recruited from Tokyo during the founder’s generation. In both looks and taste, Kyogoku Kaneyo bears traces of Japan’s east and west.

Name: Yoshokuya Fujiya
Description: The first-generation owner-chef opened this restaurant in 1935 next to his rice dealership. For four generations, this local eatery has filled the bellies of its regular customers, many of whom have been dining here for years. The hamburger patties with demi-glace sauce are a perennial favourite. The lunchtime set meals that can be enjoyed casually are a welcome idea. Miso soup and pickled vegetables play supporting roles as beloved comfort food. Good, sound cooking on which the locals were raised.

Name: Eitaroya
Description: Seafood rushed straight from the fisheries and vegetables grown by local farmers are what sell this izakaya. The white-smocked chef stands at the counter, showing confidence in his daily-changing menu. Choose how you want your seafood prepared: stewed, salt-grilled, deep-fried as tempura, and more. The sashimi plate is popular for its variety and generous portions. Sashimi is served atop a big bowl of ice, keeping the fish cool in summer and firm in winter.

Name: Sushidokoro Kaihara
Description: Omakase from a veteran of Japanese cuisine. The meal begins with grated vegetables and appetizers. Nigiri emphasises the toppings, with fish cut thick and sushi rice more modest in quantity. Smaller sushi pieces enable guests to sample a variety of fish to their hearts’ content. An ingenious twist is that the soy sauce varies by topping: shrimp is served with egg yolk steeped in soy sauce, fatty tuna with foamy soy sauce, and so on. This self-taught sushi artisan never stops learning and rewarding guests with the results of his labours.

Name: Hachidori
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Cash only,Counter dining,Notable sake list
Description: Food that pairs well with drinks and the ‘Steam-Warmed Sake’ are popular items at this izakaya. The cheerful couple who run it hail from a line of liquor-store owners. The bill of fare includes sashimi and charcoal-grilled items, with the emphasis on the quality of the ingredients, as well as dishes of Shōnai vegetables the chef procures from the production areas. The type of salt used varies, with some items seasoned with ishiru fish sauce for a twist that makes for a pleasant aftertaste.

Name: Kushi Tanaka
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Shoes must be removed
Description: A tight C-shaped counter surrounds the owner-chef. Imaginatively prepared skewers appear in rapid succession and the variety is extraordinary: mushrooms with soy butter, steamed wheat gluten with yuzu miso, bread filled with cream cheese. The prix fixe offering is called ‘Ippo Tsuko’, meaning ‘one way’, as skewers are placed in front of guests with no consultation. The owner-chef never forgets to show modesty and humour.

Name: Suigyo Murabayashi
Description: Since his apprentice days, the chef has made a habit of touring Japan to build trust with fishermen. The blessing that flows from that effort is the high-quality seafood delivered to him from each region. The first dish offered is sashimi in a large bowl. Fish of the season arrives little by little, in wondrous variety, as the sake flows nicely. Fish stew is prepared in soy sauce and water only, bringing out the natural sweetness of the flesh. The remaining broth is served with fresh-cooked rice, wasting nothing.

Name: AKA to SHIRO
Description: The chef uses two types of vinegared rice: red-vinegared rice for tuna and blue-backed fish, and white-vinegared rice for shrimp and white-fleshed fish. The red vinegar is a style popular in the Kanto region, while the ‘white’ vinegar (rice vinegar with sugar) is a Kansai speciality with strong roots in oshizushi. The combination of red and white, east and west, creates a dialogue between variations, respecting the spirit of each. Aka to Shiro also means ‘red and white’.

Name: Izuu
Description: Founded in 1781, Izuu takes its name from its founder, Izumiya Uhee, from a time when lightly salted mackerel from Wakasa was becoming popular in Kyoto, and the custom of eating sabazushi at festivals and ceremonies became common. Seeing an opportunity, Uhee began delivering these treats to the city’s geisha districts. The business passed from generation to generation, and the current, eighth generation owner-chef preserves the tradition of whole-mackerel sushi to this day.

Name: DELI a Casa
Description: The daily fare and hometown cooking of Italy mould the concept here, following the owner-chef’s passion to get people to know the cuisine he grew to love in that country. A beguiling array of appetisers are served on small dishes, after the style of a mix-and-match antipasto misto. Enjoy them bit by bit, like a tour of the regions of Italy. Simple dishes, lovingly prepared, reach deep into the soul.

Name: The New World
Address: B2F, Shinsaibashi PARCO, 1-8-3 Shinsaibashisuji, Chuo-ku, Osaka, 542-0085, Japan
Description: Its space glittering with pink neon signs and mirror balls, creates a whole new world for izakaya. In similar vein, the cuisine is genre-free: many imaginative offerings break free from the confines of Japanese gastronomy. Examples include a salad of canned mackerel and shiraae of fresh fruit in season with mascarpone. The whole restaurant abounds with originality, as the chef’s playful spirit puts smiles on patrons’ faces.

Name: Sushitsune
Description: The dish of renown here is the bateira, or pressed mackerel sushi, conceived by Sushitsune’s first-generation owner. The fourth-generation chef continues this tradition, now popular throughout Osaka, in which pickled mackerel is pressed onto sushi rice in a boat-shaped wooden frame and dressed with white-sheet kombu. With deft handling, skilfully applying just the right force to unravel the sushi rice, the chef displays the fine skill of long practice. Bozushi, of horse mackerel and conger eel, and temarizushi are exemplars of Osaka food culture. This is the place to sample true Naniwa oshizushi, beloved by ‘Japan’s Kitchen’ of Osaka.

Name: Saketosakana DNA
Description: ‘DNA’ was appended to the name to evoke the richness of Japanese cuisine and the spirit of Japan as defining features of the restaurant. There’s a reason why the soup using kombu kelp and bonito dashi stock takes pride of place. Fish is shipped directly from Obama, Fukui Prefecture, so there’s a good selection of sake from Fukui, too. Foodstuffs and sake from the same locale tend to get on well together—there’s that DNA again. The warmth of the three family members is a genetic inheritance from father to son and daughter.

Name: Tonkatsu Fujii
Description: The chef came over from the world of French cuisine to fry tonkatsu. Ingredients and cooking techniques are a complex mix of various elements, creating flavours found nowhere else. Wielding a blend of multiple oils, the chef lends his skills as a baker to the coating. Red wine accentuates the sauce. Experience inspires the ideas of this chef, who was indelibly impressed by the tonkatsu craftsmen of Tokyo. A chance meeting that changed a life, resulting in beautiful flavours.

Name: Tonkatsu KATSU Hana
Description: Only name-brand pork from various regions is used so patrons can learn what truly delicious pork tastes like. The chef is always on the lookout for new pork brands, allowing diners to sample different flavours in tonkatsu every time they visit. If undecided between the tenderloin and the pork loin, the combination platter is the way to go. The restaurant is named ‘Hana’ because that is the name of the chef’s wife. Their warm and affable personalities add to the appeal, heightening satisfaction with the fare.

Name: DEUX FILLES
Description: Owner-chef Daisuke Iwata bills his fare as ‘modern French’. His purpose in using generous portions of vegetables is to showcase the bounty of Kyoto. The salad with 30 kinds of vegetables is a perennial favourite. Selecting a white plate as a canvas, he colours it in with vegetables he buys himself in places such as Kameoka and Kamigamo. His skill in déclinaison – taking a single ingredient and turning it into sauté, sauce and powder, then serving it as a single dish – is unique.

Name: Kikunoi Mugesambo
Description: The menu of tea ceremony food conveys the flavours of Kikunoi with the culture of bento. Starting with appetisers, stewed bowls are served ryotei-style. Serving-ware—baskets, lacquer, glasses—changes with the passing seasons, laden with a colourful variety of grilled items and simmered vegetables. The house speciality, Shiguremeshi, is topped with sea bream sashimi smothered in sesame sauce. As you dine, cast your gaze over the stillness of the moss-covered garden.

Name: Vegan Ramen UZU
Description: ‘Earth-friendly dining’ is the mission of Vegan Ramen UZU. The interior artwork, created by art collective teamLab based on their theme of ‘Interconnection between humans and nature and each other’, is a perfect fit for the cuisine. Digital art that reverses left and right on the black tables, and India-ink writing on the walls, speak of harmony between nature and food, and the beauty of all creation. Guests all dine at the same table, underscoring the message that we must live and prosper together.

Name: Sobadokoro Toki
Description: Over the front door of this shop in Kitashinchi hangs a shimenawa, a twisted straw rope that wards off evil. Inscribed on a wooden block over the shimenawa is the phrase ‘Senkyaku Banrai’: ‘May customers arrive in the thousands and tens of thousands!’ In hopes the wish will come true, the doors are kept open until late at night. The sprawling menu ranges from appetizers that accompany sake to seasonal soba dishes. At lunchtime, soba accompanied by sushi is a nice surprise. In summer, chilled curry soba is brightly festooned with veggies. In winter, oyster soba in white miso soup warms the body from the inside. The special preparations for each season give something extra to look forward to.

Name: Chukasoba Uemachi
Description: The first thing you notice at Uemachi are the constant queues outside the door. The shop took the name of the neighbourhood as it aims to be a place beloved by locals. Its signature ramen dishes are ‘Shoyu’ (soy sauce) and ‘Shio’ (salt). The broth derives its richness from its meat base; the flavour of dried fermented fish and crunchy sardines add depth. Insisting on noodles with a satisfying finish, the shop kneads its own. The fare is somehow nostalgic, in both taste and presentation.

Name: Ayamuya
Description: Yakitori born from self-taught techniques and sensibilities. Different seasonings are applied to each cut; each skewer is served on a separate dish. Salt use differs by item and soy-sauce dip is enhanced with wines and spirits to build complex flavours. Interesting combinations include chicken breast dressed with grated daikon radish in ponzu sauce or horseradish and cartilage with spices. Omakase menus switch texture and flavour with each course. For à la carte items, guests can specify their seasoning preferences.

Name: Mendokoro Janomeya
Description: This ramen shop focuses on making soup using locally raised chickens. Its three signature flavours are soy sauce, salt and white broth. Be sure to try the chicken ramen. To make the signature soup, dashi is drawn from chicken bones and whole chickens. Following a time-honoured recipe, flavours are enhanced with soy sauce matured in large wooden barrels. The fragrance of the wheat is drawn out by using thin noodles. The ambience is reminiscent of the aristocratic culture of old Kyoto.

Name: Sushizen
Description: Standing in the kitchen is the second-generation chef and his son. Protecting the reputation of their restaurant as a family, father and son carry the torch for future generations. Guests’ eyes are drawn to the chirashizushi heaped with lashings of seafood. Sushi pieces brushed with sweet eel sauce are smothered in thin omelette cut into strips; this arrangement is both beautiful and practical, as it prevents the fish from drying. Oshizushi of pike conger and conger eel, futomaki stuffed with dried gourd strips and parsley are standard fare. Here the good things never change.

Name: Nihonshuzammai Utsutsuyo
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Notable sake list,Shoes must be removed
Description: The name of the restaurant is inspired by the expression ‘is this a dream or reality?” and embodies the desire for you to enjoy sake and good food to your heart’s content with a touch of enchantment. The sheer range of local sakes on offer can make choosing hard. Start with an appetiser and decoratively arranged sashimi with your first cup. The drinking snacks are varied too, from tofu preserved in miso and stew of beef tendon to Western items such as sweetfish confit and milt meunière. With such an array of appetisers, the sake slips down easily.

Name: Donostia
Description: Donostia is the Basque name for Spain’s gourmet capital of San Sebastián. Pinchos and tortillas line the glass case on the counter, reinforcing the informal vibe of a Spanish tapas bar. Dry-cured ham, marinated sardines, squid frit and other delights are served a little at a time on small dishes. Seafood salsa verde redolent with herbs and bean-and-giblet stew are standard fare. Taste country cooking rich with the distinctiveness of the Basque countryside.

Name: Oribe
Description: French bistro and teppanyaki cooking are the draw at Oribe. The impressive range of appetisers includes items inspired by French standards such as paté and smoked salmon. Its famous cabbage steak was dreamed up from the essential ingredients of okonomiyaki. Speaking of okonomiyaki, the meal ends with Osaka’s famous savoury pancake, a popular item here. The restaurant was named for the chef’s penchant for Oribe ware, and this style of pottery inspires the green theme for its décor.

Name: Bistro Cerisier
Description: French ballads warble through a retro interior, recalling the good old days. Regional cuisines such as quenelles from Lyon and cassoulet from Languedoc spill across the menu. Old-school recipes, like white asparagus with Hollandaise sauce in spring and salmis of roast mallard, bring comfort to the soul. Respect for sauces testifies to the commitment to the essence of French cooking.

Name: Fuyacho 103
Description: The name is simply the address of this restaurant hidden in a mixed-use complex. Cross the threshold and the interior is filled with the warmth of wood panelling, the coffered ceiling reminiscent of the partitions in an oden pot. The menu ranges from standard fare such as daikon radish and deep-fried tofu to more exotic choices only a former Italian cuisine chef could conjure, such as caciocavallo cheese. Taking a hint from bistecca, the steak is paired with oden dashi soup stock.

Name: Kamigata Rainbow
Description: A rainbow-coloured awning marks Kamigata Rainbow, a shop that pursues individuality even in ramen. The type of noodle differs for each type of ramen, creating unity in each. Soy sauce is redolent with lashings of small, dried sardines. In the curry ramen, curry paste floating in the soup changes delightfully as it melts. The menu includes items limited to each season, tickling one’s curiosity.

Name: Juu-go
Description: Akiya Ishibashi tills the field, harvests the grain, kneads the buckwheat. The chef’s passion for soba permeates a menu consisting purely of soba and soba mash. ‘Think of it as cereal’, he says of his dishes rich in rustic goodness. Soba is deliciously fragrant, thick-cut and al dente. Soba mash, served with roasted buckwheat grains, is delightfully pungent. To enjoy the pure flavour of Ishibashi’s soba, try it first on its own, without seasoning.

Name: Tan
Description: ‘Tan’ comes from the city of Kyotango in Kyoto Prefecture. Naturally, the food hails from the Tango region too: rice grown by employees where the restaurant was founded; vegetables from the region’s farmers. Service begins with breakfast loaded with vegetables; lunch consists of bowls of rice with toppings and noodle dishes; evening fare is à la carte. Each dish is simple yet prepared and plated creatively. The view of the willows along the Shirakawa River seen from the modern interior is wonderfully elegant.

Name: Canton Shunsai Ikki
Description: The restaurant holds its own niche in Chinese cuisine. The talents of the Guangdong-trained chef are on full display. Guangdong is blessed with the bounty of sea, mountain and river, as is Kyoto, and the light flavour of its cuisine, which draws out the flavour of the ingredients, work well with the food culture of the ancient capital. Shrimp wontons are dressed with Hong Kong soy sauce, Cantonese fried rice is accented with lettuce and roast pork.

Name: Izakaya Tokitame
Description: Before anything else, be sure to order the Obanzai Moriawase. The simple flavouring of this assortment of Kyoto cuisine side-dishes, such as shira-ae and vinegared burdock, makes a great companion for drinks. The line-up ranges from familiar offerings such as decorative sashimi and fried foods to Japanese, Western and Chinese dishes accented with a touch of creativity. The restaurant name derives from a movie about a couple who grew old together. The couple who manage Izakaya Tokitame also gather beautiful moments with their guests as time marches on.

Name: EL ALMA
Description: El Alma feels like a culinary journey, as the dishes hail from every region of Spain. The shrimp-and-mushroom ajillo represents the traditional flavours of southern Spain. Salted cod and almond sauce lend the tapas salad a Catalan flair. The meat dishes are charcoal-grilled for a smoky flavour that evokes the Basque Country. The chef, who’s made numerous trips to Spain, aims for an authentic feel that conveys the richness of regional Spanish cuisine.

Name: Sumibiyakitori Ikoka
Description: Sumibiyakitori Ikoka would like you to experience as many different cuts of chicken as possible, so a recommended start to your order is a five- or seven-piece omakase. Rather than insist on a particular brand, the owner-chef chooses poultry on quality and freshness alone. Chicken tail drizzled in yuzu and chicken skin covered in oroshi ponzu are a finishing touch. Chicken pieces prepared with slight twists are mixed together to offer a variety of flavours.

Name: Muginoyoake
Description: The chef has been researching the deliciousness of ramen since he was a schoolboy. In search of a unique flavour, he made ‘Scallop and Japanese Pepper Ramen’ his signature dish. Soup of dashi drawn from chicken, pork and seafood is multilayered and satisfying. The finished Japanese pepper oil imparts a refreshing feeling, and the generous topping of scallop is pure luxury. A carefully calibrated bowl of goodness that is the gift of repeated independent study.

Name: Izugen
Address: 391 Takeyacho, Takakuradori Ayanokojisagaru, Shimogyo-ku, Kyoto, 600-8093, Japan
Description: A Kyoto eatery to drop in often and casually. Izugen is a much-loved tradition from the old days, jealously guarded by its third-generation chef. Rice, the essential base of sushi, is cooked with kombu and bonito. Order the Kyoto sushi mixed platter and savour three styles of sushi: bo sushi with mackerel, hako sushi and maki sushi. Sushi is not hand-formed, so there’s no counter, in true Kyoto style. A picture of a maiko hangs on the wall because, the current chef says, he fell in love with it at first sight; he believes it is auspicious, as the maiko invites customers to ‘maikomu’, or ‘come in’.

Name: Ogimachi Udonya Asuro
Description: Located close to Tenjinbashi-suji, Kansai’s longest shopping street. The shop seems to be in competition for the longest queue to get in. The dish of renown is ‘Toriten to Taichikuwaten to Ontama Bukkake’ (udon topped with chicken tempura, sea bream paste cake tempura and soft-boiled egg). If the pure flavour of dipping sauce and noodles is what you’re after, try the ‘Hiyakake’. The clear sauce and delicious noodles are standouts, so the flavour of the seafood broth and the springiness of the noodles have your undivided attention. Choosing your favourite toppings adds to the fun.

Name: via del emme
Description: When the chef returned from Italy, he brought with him recipes rooted in the land and techniques for making pasta by hand. He now applies his experiences in Marche, a region rich in the bounty of sea and mountains, to the foodstuffs of Japan. Guests can choose from an impressive list of pasta dishes, some made with seafood and even game. The meat in the Bolognese sauce is hand-chopped, in a nod to Marchese practice. Always attentive to guests’ wishes, Maeda is happy to adjust flavours while hewing true to his cuisine’s Italian roots.

Name: Oryori Menami
Description: This restaurant began as a place serving obanzai and yakitori, and the sauce that the chicken and green onion skewer is grilled in goes all the way back to then. Kyoto culinary delights line the counter, such as a stew of deep-fried tofu and leafy vegetables, Kujo leek dressed in vinegar miso and boiled nama-yuba. Here you can linger and relax to the gracious hospitality of the tunic-clad proprietress, who keeps her grandmother’s name alive in the name of the restaurant.

Name: Uo China Yo
Description: The concept at this restaurant is Chinese cuisine with an emphasis on fish. First, try the set menu, with your choice of main dishes. Pick four fish dishes you like, which come with an assortment of appetisers including seafood carpaccio. This fully rounded meal even comes with fried rice at the end. Various dishes on the menu make good use of seasonal ingredients such as lobster stew with chili sauce and seafood mapo tofu.

Name: JIBUNDOKI
Description: The owner-chef pours his creativity into teppanyaki dishes of incredible variety. In true Osaka style, both pork and mixed okonomiyaki are available. Though the batter is thick, the finished texture is light. Imaginative grilled skewers hint at the cuisines of many countries, with offerings such as nama-fu, salmon tartare and tteokbokki. All items are served in bite-sized pieces, so patrons can enjoy sampling a variety of flavours.

Name: Mugito Mensuke
Description: Pursuing an original approach to ramen, the chef works with carefully selected ingredients.  Soup is prepared from free-range chicken and guinea fowl to bring out maximum flavour. Noodles, produced on the premises, are crafted for a delicious finish. Wontons stuffed with wagyu filling are the very flavour of luxury. Counter seating features an earthen wall made by a plasterer and wooden trays typical of Japanese restaurants. A ceaseless drive for improvement is evident in every bowl of ramen.

Name: Ichihana
Description: A typical lunch offering is sashimi and items served in small bowls, while the evening lineup boasts a full complement of sashimi and items served in rice and cooked individually for each guest. Ten ingredients are always available, with gomoku (‘five ingredients’) and wild plants being perennial favourites. To express the seasons through kamameshi, Ichihana offers flavours like bamboo shoots, sweetfish, mushrooms and oysters. While the rice is cooking, enjoy Kyoto flavours such as steamed wheat gluten with sweet miso sauce and steamed tilefish.

Name: Oryori Amenimomakezu
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Cash only,Counter dining,Notable sake list
Description: On a narrow alley off Oimatsu-dori, the backlit sign saying ‘Ame ni mo makezu’ (Be not Defeated by the Rain) arrests the eye. The script has a character all its own, as the owner-chef wrote it himself using chopsticks dipped in charcoal. Fare is prepared with plenty of fermented seasonings to complement the sake. Grilled fish is marinated in malted rice; chicken liver garnished with rice-bran bread. The way of living shown in Miyazawa Kenji’s masterpiece is manifested in the food on offer.

Name: Kannomiho
Description: Open the menu and the first line reads, ‘Kannomiho is the shop run by Miho, who loves warmed sake’. Miho offers home-style seasonal fare accompanied by sake and all its appeal. Seared duck is a year-round favourite. As cup follows cup, unwind as the sake warms you right through. Songs of the Showa (postwar) era pipe through the dining room. With sake cup in hand, guests leisurely soak in the pub-like atmosphere.

Name: kushiage 010
Description: These creative kushiage incorporate culinary influences from many countries. The sheer variety is endlessly fun. For your first skewer, you might start with angel shrimp from New Caledonia. The samgyeopsal (grilled pork-belly slices) wrapped in perilla and Korean lettuce is spiced with gochujang for a real Korean treat. Karaage, marinated in a sauce of spices such as star anise and five-spice powder and sprinkled with tapioca flour, fills the air with the fragrance of Taiwan.

Name: La pleine lune
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Cash only - lunch,Counter dining,Interesting wine list
Description: Chef Naoaki Nishii brings ingredients to life using traditional cuisine. One example is the thick-cut smoked salmon, paired with chestnuts in autumn and turnips in winter to emphasise the seasonal feeling. Meat dishes are garnished with kuro shichimi (‘seven black spices’) to add a Kyoto touch. In homage to classic French cooking, he does not spare the sauce, taking care to impart a modern flavouring. Butter and cream are used sparingly for a lighter taste.

Name: sonoba
Description: ‘A soba shop that makes pottery’ by a chef from an arts university. The interior sports an industrial décor, with pendant lights hanging from a ceiling made of recycled wood; a pottery studio is adjacent. Having majored in interior design, the chef was involved in the restaurant’s design and construction. Earth for the pottery, buckwheat grains for soba: both are kneaded with water, shaped and heat is applied. An unexpected point in common between pottery and food.

Name: Sambongi Shoten
Description: Char-grilled meats are the signature fare here. Sambongi Shoten bills itself as an izakaya, but the atmosphere is more like a char-grill bar. The focus is on wine being organic, sake being warm. The menu is remarkably varied, with many creations borrowing ideas from Japanese, Western and Chinese influences. Meats include beef, pork, mutton and duck, as well as game; the Miyama venison is a crowd-pleaser. The trained eye of a butcher and the flame control of a master of French cooking are on display here.

Name: Shichiku Kiko
Description: The tiled-roof row house on Gen’i-dori makes an immediate impression. The owner-chef, wearing a bow tie, rushes about, unable to rest unless he does everything himself. With his wealth of experience, he takes familiar ingredients and raises them to new levels, creating graceful Kyoto cuisine – and it’s good value for money. Appetiser platters are served with rice at lunchtime and in the evening with drinks. The gentle demeanour of the proprietress makes you feel at home.

Name: Shitennoji Hayauchi
Description: Oribe stoneware and distinctive Japanese-style paintings give presence to the interior. Crockery is produced by a potter with whom the owner-chef has cultivated a relationship. Recycled materials and earthen walls give the space a rough-hewn feel and a folk-art charm. Two kinds of soba are prepared: fine-ground seiro soba and coarse-ground inaka soba. Both are rolled to the same thickness. At lunchtime, customers start queuing in front of this popular shop before it opens. ‘Soba trays’ of soba with snacks are available with reservations.

Name: Oudon Yomogi
Description: This à la carte udon shop is a project of the proprietress of the Japanese restaurant Miyamoto. The use of bamboo gives the restaurant a kappo feel. In the evening the style is a fixed menu to which drinking snacks can be added. Great care is taken with the use of crockery – this is an udon restaurant with the flair of a soba place. The star of the udon items is the dashi soup stock, which is created with the basic soup stock, particularly drawing inspiration from soup dishes in traditional multi-course meals. A flavoursome lesson in Osaka dashi culture.

Name: NOODLE SHOP RENNOSUKE
Description: The residential neighbourhood is a maze and there’s no sign for the restaurant. A spotlight on a bowl of ramen in a showcase indicates you’ve arrived. The industrial space has the feel of a laboratory. ‘Raamen’ is a blend of Kyoto wheat noodles in a clear soup of seafood dashi stock. Thinly sliced roasted pork fillet is from Kyoto-raised swine. Blue bowls of specially ordered Kiyomizu ware set off each meal to its advantage. Custard pudding, sweetened with refined sugar, is a popular item.

Name: Sakamoto Sushi
Description: With Nishikujo Station to guide them to the spot, every evening customers gather at Sakamoto Sushi, where the familiar chef greets them with a smile. The omakase menu, which begins with a snack, is astounding in variety and breadth. Fish are painstakingly prepared by methods such as marination and searing, and are paired with white sushi rice in the Kansai way. Nigirizushi are interspersed with bozushi and hand-rolled sushi to keep things interesting. The chef uses the highest-grade fish, yet the prices won’t break the bank.

Name: Kushikatsu Gojoya
Description: The tempo in the kitchen is lively as cooks deep-fry these imaginative skewers. Order the omakase, which only ends when your belly is full. An amazing 25 types of skewers are normally available—you’ll want to see them all. Korean kimchi, Indian curry, Italian tomato sauce and so on take you on a journey from country to country. A fusion of Osaka’s fried foods with traditional cuisines of the world.

Name: Nikomi Kimura
Description: Home cooking and sake, enfolded in the nostalgic charm of a Japanese-style house. ‘Nikomi’ means ‘stew’, and stews are the chef’s signature dishes. Sukiyaki-style simmered beef and tofu, stewed beef tendon with konnyaku, and chicken meatballs are offered year-round; in winter, oden is added to the menu. ‘Fukusa Tamago’ is a rolled omelette mixed with vegetables. Western favourites such as macaroni salad and gratin can be had as well. The dishes with which the chef displays her talents are simple and full of warmth.

Name: Tempura Kozaki
Description: Tempura Kozaki expresses the seasons through ten pieces of tempura. The procession begins with tiger prawn, then alternates between vegetables and seafood. Experience in other disciplines of Japanese cuisine shines in the choice of ingredients such as deboned pike conger and Japanese mugwort gluten cake. Pieces are lightly deep-fried in cottonseed oil and served with warm tentsuyu. Frequent changes of coating show the skill of the seasoned veteran. This popular restaurant is full night after night; for the first Sunday of each month, reservations are accepted three months in advance.

Name: Teuchisoba Kanei
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Cash only,Shoes must be removed
Description: The owner-chef fell in love with soba, so taught himself how to make it. Using a stone mill, he grinds his “Rough-ground Soba” by hand to create wonderfully rustic juwari, or 100% buckwheat noodles. A shark skin grater and stick of wasabi are provided, so you can start grating your wasabi while you wait for your soba. Pre-soba snacks created with drinks in mind are on offer, including broiled miso, itawasa and dashimaki tamago. The ambience of the traditional wooden townhouse looking out on the verandah of an inner garden sets the mood.

Name: Lapintaika
Description: The menu is broad, reflecting the wide range of local Italian cooking styles the chef has studied. Each plate feeds two, so sharing is the order of the day. The assorted appetiser, generous in both portion and variety, is a perennial favourite. A full complement of pasta dishes is on offer—the list of spaghettis alone is extensive. The restaurant’s name means ‘coming back’, and indeed the satisfying weekend lunch draws plenty of repeat visitors.

Name: Itsutsu
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus
Description: As a Wakuden establishment, Itsutsu embraces their 'soba and cuisine' motto while specializing in seasonal dishes. Soba is made into thin noodles, using only the smallest amount of binder and well water from Daitoku-ji Temple. The chef doesn’t brace the noodles with cold water, so the flavour jumps to the fore. Similarly, soba dipping sauce is mild, based on its salt flavour. At lunchtime, the three-item set with soba is recommended. Mackerel sushi is a popular à la carte item. Reservations are required for the prix fixe Buddhist vegetarian cuisine, which includes soba.

Name: YI PAN CAI TANAKA
Description: ‘Yi Pan Cai’ is Mandarin Chinese for ‘à la carte’. The name reflects the restaurant’s desire for patrons to enjoy dishes they love with a light-hearted spirit. The ‘Dragon’s-Hair Rolls’ are minced shrimp and hamo rolled up in kadaif noodles and deep-fried. Dishes such as pig’s feet marinated in Tsingtao beer and deep-fried; and shumai steamed dumplings made variously of pork, beef, fish or shellfish, are creatively prepared and served as an assortment. Each dish is delightfully inventive.

Name: Rubino
Address: 53 Old Bakery Street, Valletta, VLT 1454, Malta
Description: This sweet little bistro started life in 1906 as a confectionery shop, serving, among other things, cassata Siciliana – which it still offers today. Sit in one of three cosy, traditional rooms and receive hands-on service from the owner. The blackboard menu lists classic Maltese and Italian dishes.

Name: AYU
Description: With a panoramic location near Manoel Island, this restaurant offers a unique culinary experience. The three brothers at the helm here have traveled the world, infusing their menu with global influences. Dishes like sea bream steamed with soy and ginger, and black suckling pig in a Sri Lankan-style curry, are packed with bold and spicy flavors, ideal for those seeking an exotic dining adventure. The excellent value for money and the informal atmosphere make this restaurant on Gzira’s seafront promenade a must-visit.

Name: Grain Street
Description: Situated on the main pedestrianised street in the centre of town, this restaurant with an attractive outdoor dining space serves simple, informal Mediterranean cuisine. Dishes include lasagne with squid, cuttlefish ink and nduja sausage as well as delicious desserts such as passion fruit tart with yogurt ice cream.

Name: Commando
Address: Misraħ Iz-Żjara tal-Papa, Mellieħa, MLH 1080, Malta
Description: This restaurant has a long and very interesting history, starting with the building itself (around 300 years old) and continuing with the history of the family at the helm, who have been here since 1930 and once provided support for the Royal Marines. The dining room boasts a rustic yet personalised decor with exposed brickwork and contemporary furnishings, while the cuisine focuses on fresh ingredients that are full of flavour. Our inspector particularly recommends the pappardelle pasta with a duck ragù and a few chopped hazelnuts for added flavour.

Name: Terrone
Address: Fort St. Angelo, Birgu Waterfront, Birgu, BRG 1734, Malta
Description: Tucked away on the tip of the small town of Vittoriosa, just around the corner from the Birgu seafront with its stunning yachts at anchor, this restaurant run by Maltese-Australian chef Adrian Hili serves Italian and Maltese cuisine. The superb Mediterranean-style local fish specialities include turbot with Sicilian clams and cannellini beans. As a result of ongoing restoration work, the entrance is currently to the rear of the building (not particularly attractive), but once inside the elegant decor and outdoor dining space more than compensate.

Name: Löwen
Description: Representing the fourth generation at the helm, Roman Pfaff has brought a breath of fresh air to this charming traditional restaurant; the inviting garden terrace is a wonderful spot to kick back with a view of the greenery! The quality ingredients are sourced almost exclusively from the (Lake Constance) region – information about their provenance features on the menu – but international flavours come into play too. In addition to one or two classics, the team cooks up modern-inspired dishes such as "Courgette yoghurt chilled fruit soup, lemon oil feta & almond thyme crunch" and "Roasted Allgäu carp fillet, yellow tomato and caper sugo, herb couscous". Tip: As the restaurant is very busy, it's advisable to book! There are also two rather simple but lovingly designed holiday flats right next door in the charming Hexenhäusle.

Name: Zum Vaas
Description: It is always a delight to visit a friendly and welcoming restaurant with a lively atmosphere. This one can look back on over 150 years of tradition and boasts a spruce, upscale interior. The service is cordial and attentive, and the food is delicious and made using high-quality ingredients from carefully selected producers. In addition to the menu of the day, which also features Mediterranean touches, there are the Vaas classics, such as roast Swabian-Hall pork. The impressive wine list comprises a remarkable range of vintage wines from various producers – predominantly from Germany and France, but also from Austria and other Old World countries. Comfortable guestrooms are available in the hotel of the same name.

Name: Lindenhof
Description: Like their hotel, with its cosy individually designed guestrooms, the Hankhs' restaurant is also very popular. This is down to the excellent seasonal cuisine, which has regional and Mediterranean influences. You can order à la carte or opt for a set menu (vegetarian version available). Friendly and competent waitstaff. The small terraces in front of and to the rear of the building are delightful.

Name: Zum Lamm
Description: This inn is everything you could wish for! Your cordial hosts, Ulrike and Manfred Kreger, put their heart and soul into running this popular restaurant. He is the chef and specialises in regional cuisine – one of his specialities is pike-perch from the Rhine, which is practically on the doorstep! Another equally delicious option is the herb-crusted rack of lamb with mint sauce, grilled watermelon and gnocchi. In summer, the tables in the garden to the rear of the building are in high demand. Smart guestrooms available for overnight stays.

Name: Dutters Stube
Description: The Dutter family have been running this charming 16C inn for four generations, and the seasonal and regional cuisine served here is a hit. Their Stubenrestaurant is more sophisticated (the set menu is popular); the Dorfwirtschaft serves simpler fare, such as flammkuchen and rump steak. As an alternative to the terrace, there is the pretty summerhouse. Chef Arthur Dutter is a member of the charity Deutsche Fußballköche (German football chefs).

Name: Rössle
Description: This family-run restaurant serves fresh, flavoursome cuisine made with choice ingredients. Alongside the intriguing "Chef's Menu", there are specials written up on the board, plus a menu of classic dishes – they all go down a treat. To round off your experience, attentive waitstaff, a friendly atmosphere and a delightful terrace. The attractive guestrooms combine warm wood and sleek design.

Name: DELI
Description: Here, in an appealingly down-to-earth and relaxed atmosphere, you can enjoy interesting international cuisine that is based on the seasons and drawn from select ingredients. The terrace on Niagaraplatz, a square with a waterfall feature, is also charming… The traditional hooded beach chairs are great for really chilling out. Good to know: They serve hot food all day.

Name: Weinstube Brand
Description: Here, diners can look forward to really good food which is both fresh and seasonal, as well as cordial service. Everything is pleasantly down-to-earth – just as you would expect in a wine tavern. The wine and game, like most of the produce, come from the region. Whether you opt for the classic rump steak, one of the daily specials or a vegetarian dish, be sure to leave room for the molten chocolate cake – just heavenly! Delightful courtyard terrace. In short: a fun dining experience!

Name: Krone
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace
Description: Krone has been properly invested in: from the façade to the hotel rooms, everything is chic and high quality, the restaurant is modern and sleek. The food is very good, with select produce turned into aromatic dishes with plenty of flavour. At lunchtime, a smaller range of interesting options. If you are staying longer, Basel and Alsace are very close by.

Name: Heinzler am See
Description: Whether you are in the mood for regional comfort food or something more international, the Heinzler brothers have got it covered. Their wide-ranging menu includes Swabian Zwiebelrostbraten (fried beef and onions in gravy), Arctic char and whitefish fillets, and yellowfin tuna sashimi. There is also an appealing selection of barbecue dishes with a choice of side dishes and sauces. You can choose to dine in the cosy Jagdstube ("hunting lounge") with its winning blend of traditional charm and modern design, or the lovely Panorama-Restaurant, whose large windows afford stunning views. Not forgetting the fabulous terrace almost touching the water! The waitstaff are personable and attentive – service is clearly a serious matter here. Tasteful and comfortable guestrooms available at the hotel, which also boasts a private beach area at the lake and a private jetty.

Name: Gehrlein's Hardtwald
Description: Somewhat tucked away, the Gehrlein family's restaurant boasts a warm and welcoming interior, as well as a lovely garden terrace. Meticulously crafted using the finest ingredients, the dishes served here are remarkably flavoursome. One shining example: Label Rouge guinea fowl, celeriac, carrot, miso, fritter. The friendly waitstaff pull out all the stops to ensure a perfect dining experience. The guesthouse opposite provides comfortable guestrooms.

Name: Fährhaus
Description: Practically right behind the dike and just a few minutes' walk from the ferry port, this restaurant serves distinctly local cuisine made with produce sourced from local fishers and farmers. Completely unpretentious and free from unnecessary frills, owner Gerold Janssen's dishes are brimming with freshness and flavour, as in the Helgoland crab cocktail or the crispy baked plaice fillets. Good to know: Well-kept guestrooms are available for overnight stays or holidays.

Name: Vier Jahreszeiten Restaurant Imhof
Description: You will certainly eat well at Andreas Imhof's restaurant. The cuisine is regional and uses ingredients selected with seasonality in mind. Dishes made with Allgäu heifer, for example, are popular. The interior of this friendly place is bright, refined and modern; outside, the beer garden is presided over by an impressive lime tree.

Name: Anetseder
Description: Traditional German public house culture is alive and well here, and at the same time they tap into the zeitgeist. The lovely dining space has a high ceiling and a trendy, modern feel and the waitstaff are friendly. They serve fresh and tasty food, with seasonal ingredients, preferably from the region, taking pride of place.

Name: Gambero Rosso da Domenico
Description: Domenico Cannizzaro has been on a mission to showcase Italian cuisine in Franconia for well over 20 years, and has run this restaurant at the small marina with his wife, Teresa, since 2012. Here, they live and breathe hospitality, serving two set menus, "Domenico" and "Teresuzza", which each comprise three or four courses – it's also possible to mix and match. Astute wine recommendations come courtesy of the chef-patron himself. Gorgeous terrace overlooking the Main River.

Name: Weinrestaurant Turmschänke
Description: In this restaurant in the Nicolaiturm, the lovely historical details, such as paintings and original furniture dating from 1912, foster a rustic yet elegant feel. The waitstaff are pleasingly laid-back and down-to-earth. Meticulously prepared seasonal dishes are served as a set menu or à la carte; mouthwatering options from the barbecue are also available. Complete with helpful descriptions, the wine list comprises some 140 items – most are from the region, but international labels also feature. Special wine evenings are also hosted here.

Name: Anne-Sophie
Description: We recommend getting a table in the light and airy winter garden: here you have beautiful views over the garden! The food is tasty and seasonal, with classics such as braised veal cheeks also proving popular. At lunchtime there is a reduced menu as well as inexpensive daily specials. The restaurant is located on the Schlossplatz, some 150m from the main hotel building.

Name: Gasthaus Widmann's Löwen
Description: This cosy establishment serves up classic regional fare and seasonal dishes made from high-quality, fresh ingredients. The Widmann family places great emphasis on their restaurant's connection to the region. Why not try "Widmann's spare ribs"? Alternatively, you could opt for a surprise menu comprising three or four courses? Don't miss the chance to enjoy the lovely beer garden in the summer – it really is a delightful spot! Cookery classes and various other events are also held here.

Name: Münstermanns Kontor
Description: What started as a shop selling eggs and butter later became a delicatessen and today this spot is a popular bistro with a pleasingly lively urban atmosphere and an open kitchen. The tasty dishes include German classics such as currywurst and Wiener schnitzel, but also international dishes. The food is accompanied by decent wines by the glass, and the service is friendly. Open from noon to 8pm, last orders 6.30pm. NB: They don't take reservations at lunchtime – so come early, as the place gets very busy.

Name: Westerndorfer Stube
Description: The cosy Stube of the Landgasthof Karner is a good alternative to the fine dining restaurant. The combination of rustic charm and discreet modern features makes for a harmonious whole. Here, the connection to the region is strong; from the schnitzel with roast potatoes, to the braised leg of lamb or trio of dumplings, great store is set by local and seasonal ingredients.

Name: Nußbaumerin
Description: In her cosy restaurant, Johanna Nußbaumer recreates a little bit of Austria in the heart of Berlin. Ensconced in a side street off Kurfürstendamm (aka "Ku'damm") since 2008, it has become an institution and an essential fixture. "Authentic... Traditional... Austrian" is the motto here. Tafelspitz aspic on a shallot vinaigrette, Viennese beef goulash with bread dumplings, or apricot dumplings with sweet buttered breadcrumbs are some shining examples. The good selection of wines also originates in the chef's homeland. The restaurant is popular and doesn't have an excess of tables, so be sure to make a reservation! Tip: There are also excellent options to be had at Nussbaumer Heurigen on Breitenbachplatz in Zehlendorf.

Name: Im Kittchen
Description: This little restaurant is located in the middle of the old town, in a narrow side street near the Eiermarkt. The dining area has a rustic feel and tightly packed table, which contributes to the charming atmosphere, as does the cordial proprietress, who is in charge of the service. The delicious options are written on the blackboard and also come in smaller portions as a surprise menu. The impressive wine list features around 230 labels.

Name: Scheidels Restaurant zum Kranz
Description: Conscious of their long family history (the restaurant is now run by the seventh generation), the owners here are committed to maintaining their traditions yet the food remains resolutely down-to-earth. Charming historic ambience, plus warm and welcoming staff. Simple, tasty dishes take pride of place, inspired by regional and seasonal produce. A vegetarian menu is also available.

Name: Gutshof Andres
Description: Surrounded by venerable old trees, this listed manor house has been owned by the same family since 1839. It boasts a delightful beer garden overlooking a small lake. Your hosts put everything they have into providing friendly service and fresh, seasonal regional cuisine. Their focus on sustainability is apparent in their selection of ingredients, some of which they make themselves. House-made spreads, sauces, brandies etc are also available for purchase. Should you wish to stay the night in this lovely, quiet spot, there are two flats in the former brewery, chic, modern double rooms in the coach house, and a comfortable holiday home – Gutsverwalter Haus. A practical tip: there are two charging stations for electric cars.

Name: Weißes Roß
Description: All the meat served by Hans-Jürgen Nägerl comes from the restaurant’s own butchery. This is a fact much appreciated by his guests, as are his ‘chalet snacks’ and ‘kitchen parties’. His delicious cuisine includes Tafelspitz (Viennese-style boiled beef) with herb sauce and roast potatoes.

Name: Treibgut
