Tip: Across the road, there is a terrace shaded by plane trees, right by Lake Zug and with a view of the Rigi – in fine weather the sunsets are magical!

Name: Porto Pojana Ristorante Terminus
Address: Via Poiana 53, Riva San Vitale, 6826, Switzerland
Description: A modern, elegant restaurant with an open-view kitchen, a wine cellar built into the rock, a cigar room, a winter garden and – the highlight – a beautiful terrace overlooking the lake with private mooring. The chef creates excellent Mediterranean-inspired cuisine and fish dishes, including recipes that make full use of fish from the lake.

Name: La Sitterie
Description: Here you can tuck into appealing French-Mediterranean cuisine with plenty of creative touches, spices and aromatic herbs. There are several risottos, but also a tomato tartlet with serac ice cream; crumbled Appenzell duck leg confit with savory; iced vacherin with red berries. Quality ingredients, good workmanship and a delightful landscaped garden terrace.

Name: Krone
Description: This restaurant in the hotel of the same name is located in a medieval castle complex on top of the mountain – the view couldn't be more beautiful! The stylish decor is a winning combination of modern design and historical charm. Drawing on contemporary influences, the cuisine takes its cue from the changing seasons and is made with produce sourced from Switzerland and the region. There is a gourmet menu on Fri. and Sat. NB: Due to the location, in a reduced-traffic zone, parking is available a few minutes' walk away – the hotel also provides a shuttle service (to be booked in advance).

Name: Casa Tödi
Description: Manuel Reichenbach represents the third generation of his family to run the kitchen here. The cuisine showcases regional and seasonal ingredients of the finest quality. Sustainability is also a core value at this restaurant. Take a punt on the surprise menu, which comprises four to seven courses, or go à la carte. The friendly and adept front-of-house team is managed by the proprietress.

Name: Landgasthof Bären
Description: The inviting exterior of this 17C half-timbered house gives a taste of the traditional dining rooms inside, which are lovingly decorated with high-quality furnishings. It is the garden terrace, however, that is the real highlight! In the evening, you can order an ambitious set menu, the appealing vegetarian alternative, or regional classics and modern dishes à la carte. More limited options at lunchtime. Decent wine list. Contemporary-style guestrooms.

Name: Eder's Eichmühle
Description: A terrific place that is understandably popular! The picturesque location on a hill with a wonderful garden and view of the lake is its calling card – needless to say, the terrace is a big hit in summer! Dining inside the Eder family's traditional inn is also an excellent option, whether in the more cosy dining area or in the airy, modern extension. The service is friendly and professional with a personal touch. As for the sophisticated dishes, choose à la carte or opt for one of three set menus – omnivore, vegetarian or fish and shellfish. Another stand-out feature is the extensive, top-notch wine list. Their lunch menu is also an appealing option.

Name: Tenne
Description: Your welcoming hosts run this long-standing family business with great dedication. Done out in a contemporary take on Alpine style, the cosy interior is very pleasing. The menu takes its cue from the seasons and includes some exquisite game dishes – the chef himself is a hunter! In the evening, you can choose between two set menus – one of which is vegetarian – or order à la carte. At lunchtime, the selection is a little smaller, but there is also a set menu. The appealing wine list showcases the best of the Valais region. For overnight stays, there are well-kept, modern guestrooms.

Name: AURA
Description: A stylishly urban restaurant, a top-flight events venue, a lounge or a club? AURA is a little bit of each, but above all the place to be for lovers of modern crossover cuisine with a weakness for grilled food – just watch the chefs at work! Located near Paradeplatz in the old stock exchange building.

Name: Zum Zähringer
Description: In the Matten neighbourhood, just a block away from the River Aare, this restaurant is run by Gaston Zeiter. He is originally from the Valais canton, but settled here in the lower part of Bern's old town some time ago. In the stately old building that is the Zähringerhaus, he cooks up classic French cuisine, but also dishes with Swiss influences – for example, there is fried sea bass with risotto, as well as a terrific cordon bleu. Top tip: the bargain-price menu of the day! In addition to the charming restaurant, there is a wonderful garden terrace with venerable old trees and a covered outdoor area. The wine list is also well stocked, including with numerous Valais wines.

Name: Bodega Noi
Description: A really attractive restaurant: sleek, modern, spacious and – thanks to the large glass frontage – pleasingly bright, not to mention the view of the beautiful countryside. The leafy terrace with its shady chestnut tree is also very inviting. On the menu: flavourful cuisine prepared using excellent ingredients and drawing on Mediterranean and regional influences. Lunchtime options are more limited and more moderately priced.

Name: Groven
Description: A small restaurant with a focus on simple local dishes. If you stop here for lunch on the terrace, you’ll find a different menu every day inspired by whatever ingredients are in season. There’s also a tempting selection of cheeses and game such as venison and wild boar during the hunting season, plus an interesting wine list.

Name: Chez Meyer's
Description: This elegant little restaurant charms its guests with piano music and a lovely mountain view. The classic fare comes in the form of a surprise menu that is accompanied by a reasonably priced wine list.

Name: L'Accadémia
Description: This ‘academy’ offers a good lesson in taste and delicious flavours. As such, it is the ideal place to discover top quality Italian cuisine that is fresh and tasty. This is enhanced by an ambience that is relaxed and friendly. In summer, make sure you sit out on the terrace to enjoy the view of the lake.

Name: La Cène
Description: This establishment draws the eye with its refined decor as much as it appeals with its two mouth-watering set menus: the weekly lunch menu ("Inspiration de la Semaine" – three to five courses) and the evening menu ("Éclosion des Sens" – three to seven courses), which is changed every month. Diners enjoy modern seasonal cuisine with a dash of creative flair, which keeps them coming back for more. A food and wine pairing event is also organised one evening a month.

Name: Le Patio
Description: Philippe Chevrier (chef at the Domaine de Châteauvieux in Satigny) has opted for an original twin-pronged culinary concept here based around beef and lobster, alongside a selection of traditional French bistro dishes, such as pan-fried frogs’ legs with sweet garlic, and crispy snails with mushrooms. A highly enjoyable dining experience!

Name: Kronenstübli
Description: Premium materials, tasteful fabrics and attractive pinewood panelling make for a cosy yet elegant atmosphere – just the right backdrop for the sophisticated cuisine served here, which is classic French with Italian influences. Tip: Try the canard à la presse – pressed duck – (available if ordered by at least two of your party). The restaurant is housed in the traditional and stylishly luxurious Grand Hotel Kronenhof.

Name: Haus zum Rüden
Description: This beautiful guild house on the Münsterbrücke bridge, only a stone’s throw from the town hall, dates back to 1348, as does the unique 11m-wide wooden barrel-vaulted ceiling in the Gothic Room. Dishes are based on seasonal ingredients and include classics such as Zurich-style veal and mushroom ragout in a cream sauce. Less expensive menu at lunchtime, plus a selection of dishes available in the modern bar with a terrace.

Name: Salmen
Description: A delightful place with a lively atmosphere! This elegant 19C townhouse opposite the Church of St Martin houses a charming brasserie with decorative details such as old photos, a striking chandelier and attractive parquet flooring. There is also a heritage-protected dining room with stuccoed ceilings. Chef-patron Daniel Bitterli cooks classic, traditional dishes that take their cue from the seasons and draw on Mediterranean influences. Dishes such as the sole fillets with two kinds of asparagus and hollandaise sauce exemplify the restaurant's commitment to fresh, high-quality ingredients and flavoursome cuisine. The waitstaff are very attentive, friendly and adept.

Name: Relais du Mont d'Orge
Description: Originally from Auvergne, chef Bernard Ricou was a pupil of Paul Bocuse. He extends a warm welcome at this charming, friendly place with a timeless atmosphere and a terrace commanding one of the best views of Sion. Three different classic and seasonal set menus are served. Lobster playing an important role year round and is almost always to be found on the menu.

Name: Taverne zur Krone
Description: This stately, beautifully restored historical building proposes two dining options: an elegant wood-panelled restaurant as well as a modern-style brasserie. In summer the terrace is particularly delightful. You'll find a great selection of traditional and classic dishes on the menu.

Name: Adler
Description: A little off the beaten track, this inn is delightfully cosy with its wood-panelled interior. The chef, who hails from South Tyrol, serves up classic cuisine with a modern twist, making a point of working with regional produce. The attentive front-of-house team includes his partner, a trained sommelier – the wine cellar boasts over 600 labels. There are a few attractive guestrooms available for overnight stays.

Name: Namun
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Garden or park,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: For fans of Thai food, this restaurant in the luxurious Grand Resort Bad Ragaz is the place to be! The focus is on Thai cuisine, but there are also Chinese dishes. Elegant and minimalist, the Far Eastern-style decor makes for the perfect setting. Tip: Ask about the Thai curry – even if it's not on the menu. In case you were wondering, the name Namuntranslates as "lukewarm water" and is a reference to the local thermal spring.

Name: Seven Lugano - the restaurant
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Great view,Interesting wine list,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: Situated on the rooftop of the casino and accessible via a glass-sided lift, this restaurant boasts fine views of the lake. In summer, the popular seats on the terrace need to be booked well in advance, while the lounge bar on the ground floor is perfect for a post-dinner cocktail. The cuisine here is varied and wide-ranging, both on the set menus and the à la carte, plus there’s an excellent choice of wines featuring labels from around the world.

Name: La Parenthèse
Address: Rue de l'Hôtel-de-Ville 114, La Chaux-de-Fonds, 2300, Switzerland
Description: On the road into town, enjoy a gourmet interlude in this spruce, yet unpretentious restaurant depicted by a cosy, contemporary interior and a warm welcome. The culinary score is the work of chef Gennaro Rotella, hence the Italian twang of dishes such as cappellacci stuffed with greater amberjack (fish), confit of yellow tomatoes and smoked provola. Delicately crafted, the chef’s cuisine stars regional produce like raw and cooked Seeland vegetables and beef from the Franches Montagnes district. Head to the cellar to choose your cheese, which you can wash down with a 10- or 20-year-old Tawny port. A most charming front-of-house team.

Name: Tout un Monde
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Great view,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace
Description: Situated in the heart of the village, this restaurant occupies an old 13C church that enjoys a stunning location overlooking the lake and the vineyards. Regional produce such as locally sourced meat and fish from the lake are transformed into elegant dishes, which are accompanied by equally impressive wines from the region.

Name: Du Théâtre
Description: This bistro, depicted by a stripped-back minimalist decor is conveniently located for a meal before or after a show at the Crochetan theatre. The chef conjures up creative, well-crafted dishes made from top-notch produce with regular nods to his native Italy. Dishes include specialities such as a ‘gargouillou’ of asparagus, fresh morels and spring veggies. The talented sommelier is a font of wine knowledge and fully worthy of our applause!

Name: La Muña
Description: Do you fancy Peruvian-Japanese cuisine? This restaurant on the sixth floor of hotel La Réserve Eden au Lac, on the shores of Lake Zurich, serves interesting and unfussy dishes made from top-notch ingredients. Up here you can dine in a cosy atmosphere beneath the exposed roof beams or out on the fantastic rooftop terrace – the view over the lake and the old town is magnificent! Exclusive wine list.

Name: Weisses Rössli
Description: At the Weisses Rössli, good-quality ingredients are used to create dishes inspired by French cuisine with Mediterranean and seasonal influences, including options such as monkfish with gnocchi, beetroot, radicchio and cassis. In the rear courtyard away from the street, there is a quiet terrace that can be covered by an awning. We recommend parking in the nearby car park on the Hürlimann site.

Name: KCC by Mauro Colagreco
Description: KCC stands for Kulm Country Club. The handsome L-shaped building is located right next to the ice rink and has a garden for summer days. Local produce takes centre stage in the dishes, which often draw on Mediterranean influences. As well as an appealing selection of starters and pasta dishes, the menu includes dishes for two, such as beef cutlets and lamb shoulder. Much of the food is flame-grilled or roasted over embers. The atmosphere is relaxed and the decor tasteful – the vintage sledges adorning the ceiling are bound to draw the eye! There is also a fabulous terrace. Live music and vinyl sessions provide the acoustic backdrop.

Name: Balm - La Pistache
FacilitiesAndServices: Car park,Great view,Interesting wine list,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: The elegant restaurant of Hotel Balm has a classical feel when it comes to both the service and Beat Stofer's cuisine – this is unpretentious fare made with excellent ingredients. Diners can opt for a tasting menu with four to five courses or order à la carte. There is also a well-curated wine list. In good weather, the terrace is a fabulous spot from which to enjoy the mountain views. This place is always busy, so be sure to book well in advance! Cheerful guestrooms are available for overnight stays.

Name: CAAA by Pietro Catalano
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace,Wheelchair access
Description: The location right next to an art gallery (from which you also have direct access to the restaurant) could not be more fitting, as the theme of creativity is omnipresent here in the restaurant, too. The chic, modern interior is all curved lines, with the relief of the original ceiling as its centrepiece! Pale tones and the sleek design of the tables and chairs lend a Nordic feel. All of the activity in the open kitchen can be followed by diners – in the evening, a tasting menu comprising three, five or seven courses is created here. Served at lunchtime, the three-course "Chef's Mood Menu" changes on a weekly basis. The proprietor, who happens to be the chef's sister, manages the service in concert with the chefs, and ensures a pleasant atmosphere. She is happy to provide information about the regional ingredients and the restaurant's nature-based philosophy. The cocktails and mocktails served at the bar are an integral part of the culinary experience here.

Name: Le Soleil de Dugny
Description: In this restaurant standing at an altitude of 1 000m, the friendly and dedicated family at the helm offers guests a seasonal menu that can also be ordered as a half-portion, on which numerous local products are used to create tasty classic dishes such as the speciality “local veal with Valais gnocchi”. Spectacular views of the valley and mountains, plus a stunning terrace in summer!

Name: National da Sergio
Description: A pleasant and down-to-earth restaurant in the historic old town, right next to Klosterplatz square. The former “Felsenburg” team offers classic Italian cuisine made from top-quality ingredients, including dishes such as Spaghetti Scampi and the classic Piccata Milanese. As you’d expect, Italian wines feature on the wine list.

Name: Nouvo Bourg
Description: In the heart of the historical village of Saillon, this laid-back little restaurant oozes modern bistro charm. It also boasts a very pleasant terrace. They serve three ambitious set menus (including a vegetarian one) based on the French classics and accented with modern and creative details. At lunchtime they also serve a short "business menu".

Name: Lusi Brasserie
Description: A tip before we get started: In fine weather, be sure to nab a table on the terrace in front of the building, from which you can take in stunning views of the Matterhorn! But the brasserie of the long-established Grand Hotel Zermatterhof also provides a delightful, classically elegant setting with its lovely walnut panelling and partially glass-paned vaulted ceiling. The cuisine is French and draws on international influences. The menu includes "Lusi Classics" such as calf's head, and traditional dishes such as Wiener schnitzel, steak tartare, burgers and flammkuchen – and there is always an evening special.

Name: Langosteria
FacilitiesAndServices: Great view,Interesting wine list,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus,Terrace
Description: This is the new place to see and be seen on the ski slopes overlooking St Moritz. The terrace affords magnificent views, making it a delightful spot in which to savour freshly prepared Italian cuisine. Langoustine, lobster and fish, truffle pizza and pasta are the specialities of this restaurant, which also has locations in Milan, Paris and Paraggi. If you're not skiing, the best way to get here is by taxi.

Name: Nagomi
Description: Two distinct restaurants in Les Pâquis district, run by a Japanese family: one dedicated to sushi, prepared by the father (who you can admire at work if you are seated at the counter); the other to tempura dishes cooked by the son. Both places have an authentic atmosphere, straightforward service, and top-notch ingredients: you're in for a simple treat.

Name: Les deux
Description: The chef mixes his own sensibilities into cuisine rooted in French bistro fare. The blackboard menu is a medley of authentic dishes and à la carte items made with seasonal ingredients. Generally, an appetiser and a main course is the perfect amount, but some items can be ordered as half portions, so ask your server.

Name: KIBUN
Description: The chef came from France to study Japanese cuisine, and the tale of his journey is told in his prix fixe menus, which interweave French and Japanese culinary traditions. Japanese knife techniques shine in preparing squid and pike conger, finely sliced to cut up the bones, with sauces that raise the ingredients’ taste to a higher level. Fruit and herb flavours interlace to form a cuisine that knows no borders. The ‘ki’ in the name of the restaurant is the same as the Chinese ‘qi’. The essential taste of each ingredient, expressed with consummate sensitivity.

Name: Shirokane Shin
Description: The chef queues up the first few items with a narrative arc in mind. Guests then order whatever they like from the menu, creating a programme of their own. That is to say, the chef decides the start of the meal, then guests freely request portions and flavours according to their whims on that day. With omakase seemingly everywhere these days, this show of mutual respect testifies to the thoughtfulness of the chef.

Name: Sushi Teru
Description: A brightly plastered wall catches your eye in this alley in Shinjuku Ward’s Arakicho before the cheerful owner-chef ushers you in. Service is omakase set meals only. Snacks are simple, honest fare such as seafood sashimi and grilled items. Sushi is presented in a definite order, starting with lighter flavours and working gradually toward richer ones: first white-fleshed fish such as gizzard shad, then tuna followed by conger eel, for example. The shop is named after the owner-chef’s grandmother; she stayed hale and hearty, so the name is a wish for the restaurant to have a long life.

Name: SUKIYAKI ASAI
Description: Experience sukiyaki hospitality at a counter. Standing right across from you, the server expertly prepares alternating slices of beef and vegetables. Sourced from a distinguished butcher in Shiga Prefecture, the choice beef is served in a variety of thicknesses. On the side are the signature dipping sauces: meringue-like beaten egg and rich egg yolk mixed with Tosa vinegar. The meal culminates with a final dish of shirataki noodles, stir-fried in warishita sauce and beef fat. Each dish will enchant both your eyes and taste buds.

Name: l'Odorante par Minoru Nakijin
Description: The chef sharpened his gastronomical senses in Grasse, a city in the south of France known as the ‘capital of perfumes’. Recalling his apprentice days, the chef named his restaurant ‘l’Odorante’, meaning ‘the pungent’ or ‘the aromatic’. Refined fragrance is the name of the culinary game here. Matching classic French techniques with Japanese ingredients, he fuses the two into a Franco-Japanese esprit, ensuring each dish is unique and brimming with flavour. He revels in explaining the background to his cuisine, leaving the memories of the culinary journey in all five senses.

Name: Ryuen
Description: The name means ‘swallows in the willow trees’ and it encapsulates the hope that guests will come back to Ryuen just as the swallows return to the willows each spring. The chef’s apprenticeship taught him reverence for ingredients; he learned the skill of using everything in food preparation, wasting nothing. Beef dishes are served as a middle course, taking after Oniku Karyu, Ryuen’s sister restaurant. Each dish is inventive while preserving the traditions of Japanese cuisine. The chef’s quest for new flavours embodies the spirit of onko-chishin: discovering the new by studying the past.

Name: LE PRISTINE TOKYO
Address: 1F, Toranomon Hills Station Tower, 2-6-4 Toranomon, Minato-ku, Tokyo, 105-0001, Japan
Description: This is the Tokyo outpost of Le Pristine of Belgium. Directing the kitchen is Sergio Herman, a standard-bearer in the world of Dutch cuisine. The restaurant introduces ‘New Italian’, which combines pure Italian flavours and the culinary traditions of Herman’s native region of Zeeland, in the Netherlands. The orecchiette is a true Le Pristine classic bearing Sergio Herman’s signature and is now available in Tokyo. The art and background music combine to help create a modern dining experience.

Name: Keichitsu
Description: ‘Keichitsu’ is the traditional name for the ‘solar term’ micro-season in early March when insects emerge from winter hiding – an evocation of spring, when animals awake from hibernation. The chef applies his passion to the green shoots of the natural world to conjure a cuisine bursting with imagination. Focusing on a few main ingredients, he prepares these in a variety of ways and serves them on a single plate. Vegetables, for example, may be roasted, pureed or served as a sauce, deepening their flavour. Fragrances such as yuzu citrus and Japanese pepper complement the seasons.

Name: bonélan
Description: Tucked adjacent to its sister restaurant l’élan, Bonélan offers a relaxed dining experience, where the theme is ‘classic cuisine, casual style’. Prix fixe offerings centre on modern preparations such as vegetable terrine, seafood poêle and duck confit. Offcuts are used to make consommé, sending a message about food loss. The allure of traditional cuisine, passed through a modern filter.

Name: Quatre Vingt Douze
Description: French cuisine overlays ingredients of varying flavours and textures to express a medley of tastes. That defining characteristic, says the chef, is the wellspring of his creative drive and the key to his approach in assembling his menu. Fruits, herbs and spices are all deployed to good effect and with a light touch to create his flavours. Fish and meat dishes always come with sauces, paying homage to the classics. The proprietress is in charge of the desserts. An intimate eatery from a couple who support each other like a synchronized team.

Name: DepTH brianza
Address: 2F, Azabudai Hills Residence A, 1-2-3 Azabudai, Minato-ku, Tokyo, 106-0041, Japan
Description: DepTH brianza explores concepts that broaden the possibilities of Italian cuisine. Chef Okuno’s latest culinary adventure is a taste test that takes Italian cuisine a little outside its comfort zone. While firmly grounded in tradition, Okuno enjoys reframing Japanese ingredients in creative ways. ‘DepTH’ is a play on his name: ‘okuyuki’ is ‘depth’ in Japanese. Like a wizard reworking ancient spells, Okuno dreams up imaginative cuisine you won’t find anywhere else.

Name: Sushiya Hajime
Description: The character for ‘sushi’ in Sushiya Hajime refers specifically to fermented sushi, harking back to the beginnings of sushi culture. ‘Hajime’ means ‘beginning’, expressing the chef’s desire to see the sushi world with a newcomer’s eyes, as when he used to be sent to select fish at the market. Fish is prepared according to ancient practices such as salting and simmering. Omakase set meals consist of numerous pieces of sushi formed small, affording rich variety and commitment to quality is uncompromising, which is deeply satisfying. Finely honed skills shine in attentive service.

Name: YAKITORI Moe es
Description: The chef’s pedigree in both yakitori and French cuisine shines in this restaurant’s omakase set meal. The magic begins with appetisers such as smoked chicken or terrine de foie gras. The chicken soup is like a clear consommé. The restaurant sources whole chickens of a variety that requires a long breeding period, and rests the meat for several days to concentrate the flavour. To bring out the flavour of the meat, salt is used liberally, sauce sparingly. Simple chicken soba noodles end the meal.

Name: Gendaisaryo Ginza Fugetsudo
Description: A former teahouse is now a French restaurant. Displaying their respective talents, chef and sommelier pair cuisine with wine or cocktails. Prix fixe menus are based on the 52 weeks of the year, with ingredients changing weekly, and a motif of ‘seasons.’ Fare is classic yet modern, with a focus on sauces. A full selection of Japanese and Western desserts round out this iconic Ginza confectionary.

Name: AMOUR
Description: The restaurant’s name declares respect for people, ingredients and tools alike. A sealed letter brought to your table contains a message from Chef Yusuke Goto, thanking you for visiting, explaining his approach to cuisine, and detailing the menu du jour. ‘Japanese French’ cuisine, specialising in domestic ingredients, is delicate and light and cuisine that reflects the seasons is a delight.

Name: Tokyo Chinese Ichirin
Description: Sichuan cuisine that strives for a mellow spiciness. The evening prix fixe offering, which combines steamed spicy chicken with liver paté, is highly original. We recommend adding some of the distinctive à la carte items, such as shrimp chili sauce made with whole large shrimp, or fried egg and crab as airy as a soufflé. Weekday lunches are a set menu of twice-cooked pork and dandan noodles. A popular place, so queues form at times.

Name: La Rochelle Minami Aoyama
Description: The restaurant of Hiroyuki Sakai, the famed ‘Iron Chef’ of French cuisine. On the show, resplendent in red chef’s uniform and with a pear in one hand, Sakai brought excitement to living rooms. At one time Sakai dazzled the port town of Rochelle with his ‘French cuisine à la kaiseki’. Japanese elements such as water shield and pike conger are served on artisanal plates and garnished with seasonal leaves. Bread made with rice flour is the perfect complement to sake.

Name: Ne Quittez pas
Description: Toshio Tanabe was an Olympic gymnast candidate and a professional boxer before he became a chef, steering his ambitions for the wider world towards French cuisine. His billboard reads, ‘French cuisine with seasonal seafood and vegetables’. The secret stories behind the restaurant’s name, the fish soup and the grilled clams lay bare Tanabe’s mode of living. The ‘soil course’ and the watermelon prix fixe offerings are ideas from a unique imagination. Enjoy the flavours and share in the secrets.

Name: Miyake Akira
Description: The Gifu Prefecture–born owner-chef uses his restaurant to showcase the crafts and foodstuffs of his native region. Born to a family that runs a pottery studio in Tajimi, he serves his dishes on Mino-ware vessels he made himself. Eels are beloved by the locals as they are thought to provide the stamina to overcome the famously sweltering heat of Tajimi. A bowl of fragrant grilled unagi on a bed of rice makes a fine end to the meal. A menu replete with delicacies, such as small bowls of caviar and other seafood on rice, crab served in small pots and char-grilled wagyu beef, lifts the spirits.

Name: La façon Koga
Description: “Sauce is life”, says Yoshihide Koga. His sauces are fragrant with wines such as port, madeira and vermouth. In tune with the times, he goes easy on oils and fats to ensure a clear taste. His choice of ingredients and his skill in extracting their flavour to make soup stock testify to his experience and attention to detail; curry sauce, served at lunchtime, is a culmination of a lifetime in gastronomy. Taste flavours born of true artisanal spirit, a legacy of Koga’s mentor, Noboru Inoue.

Name: Canton Meisai Akasaka Rikyu
Address: 2F, Akasaka Biz Tower, 5-3-1 Akasaka, Minato-ku, Tokyo, 107-6302, Japan
Description: This Chinese restaurant has been preaching the gospel of Cantonese cuisine for years. The richly-varied bill of fare centres around seafood, grilled items and dim sum, with whole-steamed grouper being worthy of note. Don’t pass up the steamed gyoza dumplings and siu mai dumplings. Salt stir-fry of seafood and veggies, dried abalone and stewed sea cucumber are all excellent choices as well. The goal here is to serve orthodox Cantonese cuisine. Cooking that can stand with the best Hong Kong can offer testifies to the passion of chef Hikoaki Tan.

Name: KOTARO Hasegawa DOWNTOWN CUISINE
Description: DOWNTOWN CUISINE is located in the chef’s local Satake Shopping Street. The chef arrays each table with Japanese vessels that recall memories of the working-class neighbourhood. The inspiration for the restaurant came from a world cooking contest, in which the chef competed with a concept designed to showcase the culture of Japan. Each plate is imbued with the passion to aim ever higher and the desire to thank and give back to the chef’s hometown.

Name: Hei Fung Terrace
Address: 2F, The Peninsula Tokyo, 1-8-1 Yurakucho, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo, 100-0006, Japan
Description: The exotic atmosphere is suggestive of a Chinese garden. Being part of a Hong Kong group, the focus is on Cantonese cuisine. The dim sum master creates xiaolongbao and gyoza, while the grill master serves up chicken and pork baked in iron pots. From the cornucopia of ingredients, guests can decide the seasoning and cooking style, including stewed items in oyster sauce and stir-fried items with XO or black bean sauce. Ask to sit overlooking the outer garden of the Imperial Palace.

Name: JULIA
Description: The wife is the chef, the husband the sommelier in this couple-run restaurant. The omakase set menu consists of pairings only. An evangelist to the world for Japan as a terroire, JULIA specialises in Japanese foodstuffs and Japanese wines. Most ingredients come from Ibaraki Prefecture, where the husband was born and the restaurant originated. Uniquely, the couple favours pairings of vegetables and fish with fruit. Self-taught and freewheeling, the cuisine is colourful and light.

Name: Sushi Satoru
Description: Retired pro boxer Satoru Araki is testing his mettle in a new arena. The backbone he developed from keeping his weight under the cut-off helped him overcome the struggles he faced moving from boxing ring to sushi counter. He excels in firing up the crowd. Straight from the bell, he offers eggplant sushi with a jaunty ‘oide nasu!’, a pun on the words ‘welcome’ and ‘eggplant’. Focusing on tuna, he forms the vinegared rice reverently in his fist. You’ll be knocked out by his charm and passion.

Name: L’éclaireur
Description: Ichiei Taguma was taught that a great chef is one who creates a new culinary culture. He tinkered and tested throughout his apprenticeship, honing his creativity, an experience that led him to where he is today. When he became independent, Taguma decided to focus on wood-fired cooking. Smoking by skilful tending of flame is the key to his presentation of creative French cuisine.

Name: HYÈNE
Description: Expect creative fare fusing Japanese, Korean and French culinary culture. A perfect reflection of Chef Yoko Kimoto’s life, as she carries both Japanese and Korean DNA and is schooled in French cuisine. Her speciality, potato fondant au chocolat, overlays a French dessert onto a Korean rice-cake snack her mother used to make her when she was little. Imbuing Japanese ingredients with Korean flavours using French techniques, Kimoto conjures a gastronomy that is all her own.

Name: Bouquet de France
Description: “The countryside is the foundation of French cuisine”, says Hidetoshi Imoto. He pours his labours into the flavours of rural France, such as cassoulet, a stew from Languedoc, and baeckeoffe, an Alsatian casserole. The charcuterie of pork pâtés and sausages is indispensable in expressing its home culture. Proprietress Yoko Harada’s amiable service relaxes guests with a cheerful, homelike atmosphere.

Name: Yakitori Honda
Description: The boundless curiosity of Chef Takuya Honda shines in his yakitori. The Hinai chicken he uses is aged to bring out the umami. Honda constantly tinkers with his fare through trial and error to elicit the best flavour from each cut. Unimpressed by the usual, narrow choice of salt or sauce, he broadens the selection to include condiments like condensed soy sauce, balsamic soy sauce, and rice vinegar with herbs. The chef similarly puts effort into recommending the best wine pairings.

Name: HASUO
Description: The fare here is New Korean: traditional Korean cooking with a modern interpretation. The chef applies the techniques and sensibilities he learned studying Western cooking. Banchan with 16 side dishes is a revelation. The Imperial Crepe adhering to the five flavours and five colours, is a brightly coloured treat. Ganjang-gejang, sauce-marinated blue crab, is marinated lightly to suit modern tastes. Hasuo proclaims a new Korean cuisine, raising the food of the chef’s Korean homeland to a new level.

Name: Miyawaki
Description: This counter-style Japanese restaurant dips deeply into Kyoto culinary traditions. Kenta Miyawaki’s experience manifests in fish dishes grilled in soy sauce, sake and citrus slices, or with Saikyoni, served on Kyoyaki vessels. Deep-fried tofu mixed with thinly sliced vegetables is standard fare, preserving the work of previous generations. Ingredients, which include mollusc, unagi, mushrooms and lily bulbs, change with the season. First-time customers receive omakase set meals only; from their next visit they can order from an extensive menu.

Name: IBAIA
Description: This bistro is sure to satisfy the cravings of carnivores, with French flame techniques that bring out the sizzle in meat dishes. Beef, pork, lamb and duck are cooked as hearty slabs. Their famous cutlet of beef tenderloin looks like a standard Japanese take on Western cuisine, but with a French twist: parsley and garlic are mixed in, a la lamb grilled in breadcrumbs. Here, you’ll find the thrill of savouring thick cuts of meat and the joy of opening a bottle of wine.

Name: Kappo Ryu
Description: Aiming to conjure dishes that leave an impression, the chef creates through a process of addition, umami upon umami, flavour upon flavour. Tsukuri is combined with grated onion and Tosa vinegar jelly. Boiled-down sake used in grilled items is mixed with dried sardine dashi to bring out its grain flavour. The menu eschews soups and appetiser platters in favour of wagyu beef dishes. Beef tongue in dashi vinegar and cutlets wrapped in bread are the chef’s pride and joy.

Name: DEN KUSHI FLORI
Description: A collab between the two restaurants Den, with its creative Japanese food, and Florilège, offering modern French cuisine. ‘Den’ and ‘Flori’ are joined by ‘Kushi’, meaning ‘skewer’. Yet despite the name, this is not a skewer restaurant; rather, the name reflects the experience and friendship that joins the eatery’s two partners. The fare is Japanese-Western fusion: tempura with sherry, for example, or sweetfish in baked custard tart. Always evolving, never making the same dish twice, it shows the world that experimentation makes food more fun.

Name: DA PEPI
Description: The ivy-draped façade arrests the eye. On the menu, one item after another professes the chef’s admiration for the cuisine of Tuscany. ‘Fumo’ is a dish of pasta in tomato sauce, learnt by the chef on his Tuscan sojourn. Aromas of olive oil and garlic wafting from the kitchen, tables set to encourage sharing from a single dish: it all recalls everyday life in Italy. Set menus are always an improvised surprise. DA PEPI is fun, like an invitation to dinner at a friend’s home.

Name: canade
Description: The Pinocchio doll on the shelf is a souvenir from the couple’s time in Italy. The chef studied cooking there, while his wife studied wine. Macallè-style risotto is a simple farmer’s dish, made more elegant with seasonings; Tokachi beef, from cows that have calved raised for this restaurant, is grilled over straw for aroma. The restaurant’s name is from the Japanese kanaderu, ‘to play an instrument’, and indeed the couple’s cuisine and wines make a beautiful harmony.

Name: Yuan Yamori
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Credit cards not accepted,Shoes must be removed
Description: Omakase set meals showcase the appeal of soba in all its glory. An assortment of stone mortars used to make different types of soba flour attest to the chef’s attention to detail. Buckwheat dumplings are kneaded from freshly ground flour. To keep an eye on the flour and ensure that no heat is added, buckwheat is slowly and carefully ground. Soba topped with nori seaweed is rich with the aroma of broth and nori, while mori soba is placed in the hands rather than on the table so you don’t miss any of the pure fragrance of buckwheat. Through the aroma and act of slurping rediscover the essence of soba noodles.

Name: Kan Coffee Fujifuji
Description: This intimate izakaya, run by its owner-chef and proprietress, oozes the nostalgic charm of a watering hole in old Arakicho. Both partners frequently visit producing regions and sake breweries. With the temperament of an artisan, the owner-chef pores over every detail of his dishes, which range from snacks to labour-intensive fare such as soups or fish pickled in Saikyo miso and grilled. The proprietress warms sake to just the right temperature; after dinner, she draws on her experiences to brew coffee. An unusual name for a most singular coffee shop.

Name: Tamawarai
Description: The chef is of the view that soba’s deliciousness is determined by its flour. He grinds husked buckwheat both from his garden and from farmers in Ibaraki Prefecture, catching every iota of the fresh-ground aroma. Coarse ground seiro (soba served on bamboo wicker) is full of wild flavour. Tofu soba, inspired by staff meals, and hot seiro with hot tsuyu sauce and beaten egg, are unique taste experiences. Evening service is prix fixe only, with treats such as buckwheat mash and rolled omelettes included.

Name: Sense
Address: 37F, Mandarin Oriental Tokyo, 2-1-1 Nihombashimuromachi, Chuo-ku, Tokyo, 103-8328, Japan
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Great view,Interesting wine list
Description: The chef is thoroughly versed in Cantonese cuisine and his credo is to faithfully reproduce traditional cuisine. Specialities include deep-fried whole pigeon, double-boiled premium soup with dried mushrooms and quickly-steamed star grouper. We also recommend the dim sum. Enjoy orthodox Cantonese cuisine while taking in some of the best scenery in Tokyo – there’s nothing quite like a dinner in subdued lighting against a night cityscape.

Name: Kaiseki Ohara
Description: The husband and wife in chef’s whites welcome you to their Japanese restaurant. They learned their skills at a chakaiseki (tea ceremony cuisine) establishment. While he works his culinary magic, the proprietress makes confectioneries and serves guests. Decoratively arranged sashimi of white-fleshed fish is served with a mix of rich and light soy sauce; hassun appetisers are laden with rich varieties of seafood. The spirit of the house shines in dishes that are uncluttered, meticulously crafted and honest.

Name: Shizuru
Description: A kappo with service by a couple in chef’s whites. Having both studied Kyoto cuisine, this husband-and-wife divide cooking duties between them. The husband prefers subtler seasoning, always to be accompanied by local sake from Yamagata. The rice, Koshihikari from Uonuma, is delivered from the proprietress’ hometown, cooked in a broad-rimmed cooking pot and patiently transferred to a wooden container. The aroma of incense wreathes the shop in a gentle, quietly soothing Japanese ambience.

Name: LE BOURGUIGNON
Description: Evoking Burgundy, the name of the restaurant comes from the owner-chef being inspired by the passion of the restauranteur and wine producer where he trained, an influence also evident in the rich selection of wines from Burgundy. His specialities include boudin noir with apple salad and purée, and millefeuille-style horse crab, eggplant and avocado. He also does wild game and offal well.

Name: ARMANI / RISTORANTE
Description: Creative cuisine, a fusion of Japanese and Italian food cultures, graces the tables of this contemporary interior. Pasta in the shape of rice and risotto using domestically grown saffron attest to a culinary sense bursting with imagination. Carbonara and tiramisu prepared with updated techniques offer fascinating glimpses of a modern cuisine evolved from time-honoured tradition. The refinement for which the Armani brand is famed provides a fitting venue.

Name: Tsunokamizaka Koshiba
Description: The owner-chef learned his trade from a master of the Kansai school, and that experience shines in his dashi stock enriched with kombu kelp and his amuse-bouche of rod-shaped pressed sushi of chub mackerel. Appetisers are indispensable to the menu out of respect for time-honoured craftsmanship, but also to delight guests with a cornucopia of drinking snacks. A wide variety of grilled items and rice dishes offers plenty of choice. Diner satisfaction is the top priority here.

Name: Tokihami
Description: A kappo izakaya bursting with creativity. The extensive menu captures your attention with its blend of Japanese and Western styles. Sansho pepper simmered in oil becomes ajillo à la Japonaise with seafood and unripe pepper. Popular items are lavished with delicacies: monaka wafers stuffed with foie gras, for example, or truffle omelette. Tsufuhan (‘Gout Rice’) is an ensemble of salmon roe, salted and dried grey mullet roe, sea urchin and caviar. Opulence that piques one’s curiosity.

Name: nerisa
Description: Tonnato of veal, hand-rolled tajarin pasta, agnolotti: Chef's experience with the cuisine of Piedmont is everywhere on display. He stays faithful to the recipes he learned, because he wants guests to know the taste of true Piemontese cuisine, but he links Italy to Japan by incorporating local ingredients. The accent in cooking is on simplicity and his personality shines in his line-up of ingredient-focused fare.

Name: Takumi
Description: Each dish arrives with a card explaining it. The Chef was inspired to adopt this approach by the way art galleries convey the concepts behind their artworks. Exploring unusual combinations of ingredients, he uses spices and herbs to assemble layers of flavour and fragrance. From temperature to texture, everything is calculated to create a cuisine that is by turns simple and complex. All five senses are satisfied, leaving a lasting impression.

Name: Le Coq
Description: Simple cuisine that emphasises ingredients leaves a lasting impression of flavours and arrangements. Thick-cut smoked salmon is one example. A veteran chef, Mitsuhiro Hiruma focuses his skills on delicious preparations with nothing extraneous. The restaurant’s name is French for ‘rooster’, the symbol and national bird of France. Having honed his technique in local restaurants, Hiruma expresses this precious experience in his cuisine.

Name: Asagaya BIRD LAND
Description: Piped jazz fills the air at this little counter wrapped around a grill. When his mentor let him open up his own branch, the chef put down roots in Asagaya. Emulating his mentor, he grills Okukuji Shamo chicken, pairing it with wines. Prix fixe menus alternate between chicken and vegetables. The value of the rare chicken cut known as the ‘oyster’ was revealed in this area as well, leading to its popularity. Free-range chicken as you’ve never tasted it.

Name: Arakicho Tatsuya
Description: The owner-chef prides himself on being the link between diner and food producer. He visits not only the producers of the ingredients he uses, but also the potters who make his crockery, sake breweries and wineries, building strong and trusting relationships. To convey that background to his guests, the chef goes the extra mile to make the dining experience fun. Meals conclude with risotto-like rice soup made with broth from takiawase. The chef is determined to waste nothing, using every morsel of food—a commitment he delivers on with flavours that warm the soul.

Name: BIRD LAND
Description: BIRD LAND enchants guests with its wonderfully distinctive yakitori. With supple imagination and a wealth of experience, Toshihiro Wada crafts a new world of possibilities for the humble skewer.  Included among the skewers in his set menus are liver paté, chicken grilled in pepper and oyakodon (chicken and egg on rice). Always attentive to customers’ voices, he reveals the value of rare cuts such as chicken oyster. Determined to pass on his skills, he often works the grill with apprentices at his side.

Name: THE UPPER
Address: 10F, MARUNOUCHI TERRACE, 1-3-4 Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo, 100-0005, Japan
Description: Dining on the top floor of a tall building surrounded by other high-rises, the view from the spacious rooftop terrace will leave you spellbound. The chatter of guests and the unpretentious service mirror the day-to-day vibrancy of the metropolis below. Regional dishes such as escargot, quenelle and cassoulet are fine companions for wine. Experience a typical day in France in a contemporary Tokyo setting.

Name: La Brianza
Address: 3F, Roppongi Hills Residence C, 6-12-3 Roppongi, Minato-ku, Tokyo, 106-0032, Japan
Description: Here, Italian recipes meet Japanese ingredients. The fish carpaccio is subtly flavoured with kelp, while the focaccia is served with a yuzu pepper sauce; the risotto is made with Japanese rice. Both Italian and Japanese cuisines celebrate the four seasons, incorporating unique flavours into every dish. While set menus remain the focus, La Brianza also offers à la carte dishes in the evening, allowing diners to tailor their culinary journey.

Name: Oryori Katsushi
Description: The owner-chef’s obsession with dashi soup stock was learnt from his mentor, a Kansai native. He mixes dashi of dried bonito flakes, kombu kelp and clams to impart depth and richness. This dashi is found throughout: in savoury egg custard, soup dishes, hot pots and other Japanese favourites. The chef’s choice of career is down to the influence of his brother, a sushi chef, and this brotherly bond is shown in his vinegared rice, simmered abalone liver sauce and pressed chub mackerel sushi. The menu is a stage on a fascinating journey that we’re going to keep watching.

Name: Äta
Description: The appetiser is a seafood charcuterie: squid and mussels dressed in aioli, finely minced raw horse mackerel, and dried chub mackerel. Be sure to try the speciality, bouillabaisse with a rich seafood flavour, and mix it rice with the leftover soup to make risotto. This is a bistro for enjoying seafood to your heart’s content, although the mains include meat dishes as well.

Name: Kagurazaka Marutomi
Description: Wagyu beef is the tie that binds the family of Kenichi Onodera. He named his restaurant ‘Marutomi’ after his grandfather’s cattle farm, and his parents ran a butcher’s shop in Ichinoseki. For that reason, he focuses on wagyu from Iwate Prefecture. Char-grilled and fried items are on the menu, as is sukiyaki with edible wild plants and matsutake mushrooms. The menu changes twice monthly, so a wide range of ingredients are sourced. The combination of traditional multi-course meals with beef dishes is pure Onodera.

Name: Benoit
Address: 10F, La Porte Aoyama, 5-51-8 Jingumae, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo, 150-0001, Japan
Description: The Tokyo outpost of Benoit, which was founded in Paris in 1912. The cuisine of this bistro that co-stars French and Japanese influences is overseen by Alain Ducasse. The menu is prix fixe, but diners can choose items to their liking. Dishes bequeathed by the Paris flagship, such as oven-baked escargot and terrine, stand alongside regional fare made with ingredients from across Japan. Antique-accented décor and attentive service convey an unmistakeably French esprit.

Name: bistro simba
Description: Visiting France in the 2000s, chef Kikuchi was deeply impressed with the ‘bistronomy’ that was sweeping Paris at the time. He made up his mind to focus on this fusion of casual bistro fare with refined gastronomy. Bouillabaisse rich in the flavour of shrimp and Paris-Brest, a pastry, are prepared with loving memory of Kikuchi’s mentor. Committed to “simple, aromatic food with friendly service”, Kikuchi is moving forward.

Name: Tempura Asanuma
Description: Fascination with Edo culinary culture led this chef to open a restaurant in Nihombashi. Knowing that Edokko (natives of Tokyo) would eat thick-battered tempura soaked in sauce, the chef uses the technique completely opposite to the thin coating he learned as an apprentice. But the thicker coating traps air bubbles, imparting a fragrant nose and light texture. In an homage to the port of call where tempura arrived from Portugal, the fried feast begins with shrimp toast, a speciality of Nagasaki.

Name: Sushi Matsumoto
Description: The atmosphere is relaxed, with jazz playing in the background. To ensure the most enjoyable sake experience, the chef alternates between snacks and nigiri. This is a great place to try a variety of sakes, served in glasses and accompanied by an extensive selection of snacks and sushi. Toro (fatty tuna) is served first, so that the heat of the freshly cooked vinegared rice melts the fat.  Fresh-toasted nori and tea served in Nambu ironware teapots show commitment without compromise.

Name: commedia
Description: Seating is counter only, and everyone begins at the same time. After starting with cured ham and cheese, a succession of homemade pasta dishes follows. Meat is char-grilled wagyu sirloin. To wrap up the evening, dishes from dried noodles bring joy to pasta lovers. Mr and Mrs Yamaguchi recreate the cheerful fun of a typical day in Italy, as befits the name commedia, ‘the comedy’. Their desire to bring joy to customers comes through naturally from their cuisine.

Name: Arva
Address: 33F, Aman Tokyo, The Otemachi Tower, 1-5-6 Otemachi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo, 100-0004, Japan
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Car park,Great view,Interesting wine list,Wheelchair access
Description: Chef Masakazu Hiraki’s aim is to create Italian dishes showcasing the appeal of Japanese ingredients. His work is a cross-fertilization of the knowledge of Japanese farmers with his own experience in Italy, particularly in the Veneto region. Vegetables and fruit bring lively colour to simple, modern fare. His devotion to the good things of the earth manifests in his restaurant’s name, which means ‘harvest’. The stunning view from his dining room atop a 33-floor building adds to the feeling of spaciousness.

Name: LA BONNE TABLE
Address: 1F, Coredo Muromachi2, 2-3-1 Nihombashimuromachi, Chuo-ku, Tokyo, 103-0022, Japan
Description: LA BONNE TABLE lives by the motto ‘farm to table’. Chef Kazunari Nakamura builds strong relationships of trust with food producers, who ship ingredients to him directly from their farms. An amuse-bouche, appropriately named ‘Farm to Table’, is a colourful assortment of vegetables prepared in a variety of ways. Roast shiitake wastes no part of the mushroom, not even the stem. The chef’s ingenuity and creativity bring out the value of his ingredients.

Name: O2
Description: ‘O2’ (‘oh-two’) is a play on Chef Otsu’s name. Like his bow tie and denim apron, the pun is an Otsu trademark. Presented as Chinese cuisine, the fare at O2 really defies easy categories, making use of both Western and Japanese ingredients. The chef’s code is to use Chinese elements in both technique and seasoning. The playful interior also expresses Otsu’s unique vision.

Name: Azabu Wakei
Description: The aim here is to serve Japanese cuisine that stands the test of time. To add an inventive touch to fare handed down over generations, repeated innovations seek new taste sensations while preserving the basics. Decoratively arranged sashimi consists of conger eel grilled over straw and dressed with caviar; tuna is coupled with a starchy nori seaweed sauce. The owner-chef’s principle is that “cuisine is made by people to be eaten by people”. Wakei seijaku, or ‘harmony, respect, purity and tranquillity’, a spirit of mutual respect between chef and guests, pervades the atmosphere.

Name: JINBO MINAMI AOYAMA
Description: Modern Italian fare that makes abundant use of vegetables. Chef Yoshinaga Jimbo visits farmers throughout Japan to paint scenes of pastoral life through his cooking. The bagna càuda theme is the breath of the seasons. Brilliantly multicoloured platters and light flavours are the strong points here. As a proud supporter of his home region, Jimbo sources many ingredients from Ibaraki Prefecture, fulfilling hometown expectations as an Ibaraki Food Ambassador.

Name: BON CHEMIN
Description: The name, which means ‘good road’, reflects Ryo Hanazawa’s determination to tread the path of the culinary artist with sincerity.  His theme is universal flavour and his methods are based on the recipes of the legendary restaurateur Auguste Escoffier. Sardine and vegetable soup, and pigeon and duck roti with offal sauce are long-time favourites in which he takes special pride. Japanese ingredients give a unique twist to his dishes as they bring back the aroma of the good old days of French cuisine.

Name: Asakusa Nagami
Description: Asakusa is the stage on which chef Takumi Nagami performs. Staying faithful to the native flavours of his ingredients, he brings to bear the seasonal elegance he learned in Kyoto. Soup stock is lightly seasoned so as not to overpower the main ingredients. Two options are available for appetiser platters: drinking snacks adorned with leaves or served in hollowed-out yuzu fruits. The kaminari-okoshi sweet rice puff snack is used as batter for fried items, in a tip of the hat to the chef’s beloved Asakusa.

Name: Pont d'Or Inno
Description: The name ‘Pont d’Or’, literally ‘Golden Bridge’, is a wish that French cuisine and the district of Nihombashi will both prosper. Tasteful décor, reminiscent of a European house, oozes panache. Chef Ken Yuhara incorporates Japanese elements into classic French cuisine taught to him by Noboru Inoue. Manager Toru Ozaki regales guests with explanations of each dish, his attentive service adding to the meal like a floral bouquet. A golden bridge anchored by three talented partners.

Name: sio
Description: Remixed music plays in the background of a dining room which has the feel of a vintage café. The venue is popular for its simple, casual style. The young, close-knit team puts guests at ease with their friendly service. Cuisine is based on French fare but interweaves influences from Italian and Japanese cooking. This is genre-free cuisine born of multinational creativity.

Name: Sushi Taichi
Description: This restaurant loves the chic style of Edo culture and values the human touch. Many sushi shops these days offer two time-limited seatings, serving only omakase set meals. However, Sushi Taichi shows the mettle of an old-fashioned sushi chef. The owner-chef’s agreeable disposition ensures him many regular customers. Above the counter is a shop curtain, while the walls feature woodblock prints depicting street stalls. If you like old-school sushi shops, Sushi Taichi is for you.

Name: MASIA
Description: Masía is Spanish for ‘farmhouse’. The chef, Mateu Villaret, created the restaurant from his roots, the dining table of his family back in Catalonia. Inspired by the Mediterranean Sea and the Pyrenees, the hometown fare combines ingredients from both sea and mountain – and proves that Japanese seafood and Spanish ham and chorizo go very nicely together.

Name: Hikarimono
Description: Kan Sato, known affectionately as ‘Satokan-san’, loves hikarimono (literally ‘shining thing’: fish with silver skin, sliced with the skin left on), hence the shop’s name. The menu is composed with drinkers in mind, so this hikarimono is never left off. Sato’s offering of three courses—sushi and bar snacks, mainly nigiri, and bar snacks—as well as à la carte is pleasing. Hikarimaki of pilchard, shredded dried plum and bettarazuke (daikon pickled in salted rice malt) is famous. Sato’s aim is to offer a sushi shop where people drop in casually. The value for money truly shines.

Name: Chugokusai Kan
Description: Owner-chef, a Keio University graduate, became a chef from his dreams of being an artisan; a person who can accomplish one thing can do anything. Flame-broiled items finished in the massive oven are a gift acquired through many labours as a hotel chef. Fujii cuts a deft and poised figure in the kitchen, master of both theory and practice. He claims his mother vehemently opposed his choice of career, but when he beholds the joy of his guests, his face is the picture of happiness.

Name: GINZA HABSBURG VEILCHEN
Description: Shingo Kanda is spreading Austrian culinary culture. Giving top billing to the cuisine of Vienna, Kanda serves traditional fare from each state of Austria. Wiener schnitzel and boiled ham are typical Viennese specialities. Kanda happily explains where he gets his recipes and tells anecdotes, explaining a cuisine unfamiliar to many of his diners. This dining experience is sure to spark your desire to visit Austria.

Name: Sushi Kagura
Description: The chef was drawn to sushi by the simplicity of a dish that is complete with only vinegared rice, wasabi, and a topping. Labouring as an apprentice from dawn to dusk, Kagura’s chef gained a thorough grounding in work that was faithful to the basics. As he moulds his sushi, the chef adds a unique interpretation to the techniques he learned.

Name: Takahashi
Description: After studying kaiseki cuisine, the chef moved to Singapore to spread awareness of Japanese cuisine. He returned out of renewed appreciation for the quality of Japanese ingredients. Exceptionally particular about his ingredients, the chef refuses to trust them unless he inspects them at market himself. He learned the basics at famous restaurants in Japan, then acquired hospitality skills from his experience overseas. Both qualities reveal themselves in his fare and service.

Name: Chiso Koryu
Description: The restaurant’s name declares that its food is created, not merely prepared, and indeed the cuisine here is infused with imagination. Kazuki Takagi spares no effort to furnish a delightfully creative bill of fare, casting his magic on ingredients from around the country. Puffer fish spring rolls, monaka wafer cake filled with monkfish liver and smoked daikon pickles testify to his inventive spirit. Sesame tofu and sea bream on rice with Japanese tea poured over it follow tradition.

Name: Sanwa
Description: ‘Sanwa’ means ‘three-part harmony’: harmony between producers, chefs and guests. Descending the stairs, your eye is caught by the three-ring logo, which is both the Watanabe family crest and the restaurant’s symbol. The menu lists producers by name, neatly linking them to guests through the chef. The name would not suggest an Italian restaurant, nor does its offering of char-grilled meats, but these speak to its unique character. The strength of three brings mutual prosperity.

Name: Arakicho Kintsugi
Description: An intimate Japanese restaurant that fits well among the string of watering holes in the Arakicho area of Shinjuku. The two who run it are experts in cuisine and sake. Set menus are plotted with the tastes of sake drinkers in mind. One piece at a time, in small quantities, is an enjoyable way to dine. As the sake flows, boiled greens, sushi, fried items and other items are served with varying degrees of preparation and temperature. A seasonal selection of steamed items on rice ends the meal.

Name: Jimbocho Gokita
Description: Yuto Gokita is pioneering yakitori eaten with French sauces. In place of yakitori dipping sauce, Gokita favours Madeira and red-wine sauces prepared from chicken bones and calf broth. Skewers of chicken breast and shrimp are smothered in sauces of crustaceans. Skewers of chicken meatballs are accented with herb butter for a Bourgogne flavour. Reservations are required for the set menu which includes wood-grilled lamb and pigeon.

Name: Nebuka
Description: Nebuka was opened by the proprietor of a wine bar. It is said that the best grapevines are those with the deepest roots (‘ne-buka’), and deep are the connections Nebuka cultivates with producers and in ingredients and cuisine. Omakase set menus focus on vegetables and game. Experienced in both French and Japanese cuisine, the chef applies expertise in both schools, and even creates pasta dishes. Each dish is arranged simply, placing the ingredients centre stage. A young team provides bright and pleasant service.

Name: Tasogare
Description: Tasogare means ‘twilight’, and that’s when the doors open, to ensure guests an enjoyable visit. Fun is on the blackboard menu, with combinations that make visions of deliciousness dance before the eyes - foie gras with Danish pastry, for example, or asparagus with zabaglione. Vinegared fish and stew are the very essence of Japanese cuisine. Tasogare entices with layers of nuanced technique and a spirit of playfulness. Free-spirited cooking, to be enjoyed with a free spirit.

Name: Oryori Kokoroba
Description: The name incorporates a character from the chef’s name while professing sincere devotion to gastronomy. That sincerity is on full display in the hassun appetisers. To convey the mood of the passing seasons, the chef incorporates meticulously chosen items fresh from the market. Oyakodon (chicken and egg on rice) made with freshly cooked rice is a sentimental favourite of the chef, one he’s made continuously since his apprenticeship. His dedication shines through in his painstaking attention to his work.

Name: Chugokusai KAKYU-BOU
Description: Huaqiu (read as Kakyu in Japanese) is the name of a holy mountain, mentioned in a Chinese book of philosophy, where many fruits grow. The name Kakyu-bou, ‘Kitchen of Mount Huaqiu’, captures the joy of cooking in a spirit of thanksgiving for the foods granted by the gods. As an apprentice, the chef learned that without the basics there can be no application. Accordingly, he searches for innovation while staying within the boundaries of orthodox Chinese cuisine. The appetiser assortment consists of bounty from sea and soil prepared with Chinese techniques. The joy of cooking creates the joy of eating.

Name: RISTORANTE la primula
Description: A counter-style Italian eatery presented by a chef who learnt his trade in northern Italy and an owner who loves all things Venetian. Tapestries recreate the canals of La Serenissima; Venetian glass and Carnevale masks variegate the interior. The northern penchant for butter influences the chef’s culinary stylings. Homemade pasta is cut thick, after the chef’s preference: the tagliolini is the product of a seasoned artisan.

Name: Alternative
Description: Alt-rock is rock music that doesn’t fit any particular category or is born of a spirit of breaking down established concepts. Noting the free rein Gallic cuisine enjoyed during his sojourn in France, the chef named his restaurant ‘Alternative’ to signal his determination to create new value. He lays the foundations of classic French theory and technique before adding elements from Japanese and Chinese culinary traditions. The venue, the former premises of a neighbourhood workshop, also expresses the chef’s individualism.

Name: Chugokusai HINA
Description: Counter-style Chinese committed to natural deliciousness. The husband, schooled in the kitchens of Yokohama and Shanghai, focuses on the cooking, while his wife serves guests. The inherent flavours of the ingredients are held paramount, interpreting the seasons of Japan through Chinese cuisine. Each dish is seasoned with restraint and elegance. In a novel twist, instead of Shaoxing wine, items are paired with well-aged Japanese sake or organic wine.

Name: Kabukizaura Masashi
Description: Diners are greeted by the open owner-chef and the graceful proprietress. The playful riot of colours on the wall is a tableau on the theme of people’s relationship with food. In this vision stretching from the past to the future, faces are drawn in kumadori, the shaded kabuki makeup fitting for a restaurant ‘behind the kabuki theatre’ (kabukiza-ura). The omakase set meal abounds in changes in inflection: two pieces of nigiri and two types of fried items (tempura and deep-fried) highlight contrasting textures. The chef’s experience with Chinese cooking bursts from his baked gyoza. For the best drink pairings, let the proprietress choose.

Name: DAN
Description: Casual French dining by a chef with deep experience in gastronomy. The counter forms an arc around the kitchen, dissolving the barrier between host and guest. Traditional recipes cooked with Japanese ingredients highlight the affinity between the two. Risotto, for example, is a perennial favourite, being a rice dish. The intimate establishment and cheerful circle of guests make Dan a step up.

Name: Toriyaki Ohana
Description: A menu that is all about chicken in the traditional kaiseki multi-course meal style, from a chef accomplished in Japanese cuisine. Start with an appetiser of chicken breast wrapped with nori seaweed or spring roll of minced chicken with miso. Soup dishes are stocked with chicken wonton. Grilled chicken and duck are not skewered but char-grilled on a wire net, pungently scorched on the surface by broiling close to a hot flame. Chicken bone soup over rice brings down the curtain. Nothing is wasted, proving that every part is delicious.

Name: Orchestra
Description: Imola, the city in Italy’s Emilia-Romagna where the chef apprenticed, has a famous music academy. The restaurant’s name derives from the passion for classical music he learned from the students he befriended there. In Imola, the chef developed his belief that a restaurant resembles an orchestra, in that a wide range of players work in harmony to create a greater whole. Cuisine on plates decorated with musical instrument motifs and classical music piped into the dining room deliver a performance worthy of any conservatory.

Name: misola
Description: Sky blue is the colour theme of misola. Framed by azure wall, objets d’art of birds take flight. Seafood is the chef’s forte, owing to his experience in Venice. A prix fixe presentation begins with paste of salt cod, a famed local dish from Italy. Vegetables are gathered fresh each morning; meat dishes are light and delicate. Simple yet inventive, misola is the evolution of Italian cuisine.

Name: 124. KAGURAZAKA
Description: The numbers in the name are both the address of the shop and the birthday of a member of staff. The first skewer is chicken heart, because the deep, rich flavour of this cut makes a strong impression. norimaki (bite-size chunks wrapped in nori seaweed) of chicken tenderloin, cooked vegetable salads and deep-fried tofu intersperse the omakase set meal, varying the tone and providing items that pair agreeably with sake. Ramen in chicken broth closes out the presentation. Served in dragon-pattern bowls with nori to evoke a certain sense of nostalgia.

Name: hatsune
Description: The chef works alone in this tiny restaurant. At lunchtime the predominant theme is noodle dishes, such as dandan noodles and hot-and-sour ramen. In the evening, both à la carte and set menu dining are available. Be sure to order the appetiser platter, as it’s packed with variety and the time and effort taken to prepare it are apparent. The spring rolls, a finger food, are also recommended. The ‘Yellow Mapo Tofu with Seafood’ intrigues with its unusual name and distinctive yellow colour.

Name: Chez Inno
Description: Chez Inno is a creation of Noboru Inoue, a name engraved in the history of French cuisine in Japan. Responsible for the kitchen, Koga and Teshima carry on his ambitions. This restaurant raises the bar in gourmet dining, as witnessed in the lamb à la Maria Callas, the founder’s reframe of a venerable recipe. The sense of what must be preserved and what should be tinkered with is astute. It will be a joy to see how the new Chez Inno changes.

Name: Valinor
Description: The chef aims for nothing less than unforgettable cuisine. His ingredients are the stars of his show, and to place them at centre stage, each dish uses as few as possible. While adding twists to texture and flavour, he leaves a vivid impression of each ingredient. Only those dishes that keep being made, keep being eaten, can be called classics. He puts his stamp on his food through simplifying the complexities of French cuisine.

Name: KOKYU
Description: A ‘food laboratory’ housed in a small, renovated warehouse. Only creative cuisine, fragrant with spices and suffused with the umami of tea, for pairing with cocktails is offered. Recipes take their inspiration from French cuisine and the restaurant’s name, which means ‘wither and decay’, is from the desire to breathe deeply of love for old cuisine before creating the new. Enjoy the fruits of experimentation in cooking and beverages.

Name: Wakiya Ichiemicharo
Description: The flagship restaurant of Yuji Wakiya, renowned pioneer of nouvelle chinois cuisine. With “tradition and creativity” as his motto, Wakiya professes a new style of Chinese cooking. The starter, ‘Nine Joys Assorted Appetiser’, is so named because nine is a number believed to bring good luck in China. The restaurant name means ‘once a day, let’s relax, laugh and have tea’. Cuisine and hospitality to bring a smile to your face.

Name: Tanakada Nishiazabuten
Description: From the Rosanjin crockery to the retro Showa-era coasters, Tadaaki Tanaka’s restaurant is an interplay between authenticity and playfulness. The comments on the menu are easy to understand, enticing with delicious descriptions. When the chef exclaims “Tabetenshai!” meaning “let’s eat” in the Hakata dialect, it makes you want to eat what you like, as much as you like. The courteous staff of this high-grade izakaya, a step above a kappo but not quite a ryotei, ensure you’ll enjoy your visit.

Name: Kappo Yuichi
Description: This counter-style restaurant hangs out its shingle in a corner of the roundabout in front of the north entrance to Ogikubo Station. Chef Kotaro Tachibana bases the menu around vegetables, showcasing the depth of Japanese cuisine. Takiawase highlight the ever-changing faces of nature, with colourful vegetables that cool you in summer and warm you in winter. Appetiser platters arrayed with salad with mashed tofu dressing, seasoned boiled greens and vegetables dressed with sesame sauce calm the soul still further with their savoury flavours.

Name: Uisane
Description: What Kohei Ikeda tries to do is mix freewheeling imagination into traditional fare, an approach taught by the head of Kikunoi during his apprenticeship there. Fine examples include sea urchin wrapped in sea bream and spring rolls of glass shrimp. He focuses on ingredients from his native Ehime, the better to share its wonders with the world. Born and raised in Uwajima, Ikeda dreamed of becoming a chef in his youth. He never forgets to carry out this ‘original intention’, a phrase reflected in the name of the restaurant.

Name: Sushi Kanesho
Description: Akira Watanabe inherited old-school sushi traditions but learned from his mentor the spirit of adding his own novel spin. Vinegared sushi rice is regarded as the most important component of great sushi, and Watanabe’s evolved over time through trial and error. The chef displays judgment and skill as he serves gizzard shad first, and his simmered conger eel and kurakake egg (egg straddling the rice like a saddle) reflect his personality. He confides that he tries to ‘investigate the old and understand the new’.

Name: UDATSU SUSHI
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus
Description: A fresh intersection between sushi and art. The walls of this modern space are hung with paintings by artists, giving the feeling of dining in a gallery. Bright and colourful side dishes include herb rolls, smoked tuna and veggie rolls. Nigiri technique hews close to the basics, but with some tempura-inspired creative touches, such as sea urchin and fried nori. A sushi restaurant for a new age.

Name: Maeshiba Ryoriten
Description: The speciality is charcoal-grilled beef and sauce only. On this, the French cuisine of Taira Maeshiba is focused. Ingredients whose producers are listed by name, finely disciplined flame-tending techniques, and traditional yet distinctive sauces combine to form menus only Chef Maeshiba could compose. The fare is simple, the work meticulous.

Name: Sudachi
Description: This Japanese restaurant offers puzzles and coded menus! The puzzles rely on a coded-language tradition called goroawase, so if you know a little Japanese, they are sure to raise anticipation. Counter seating, which affords a view of the food-preparation process, adds a touch of fun as well. The eatery’s name can mean ‘leaving the nest’, and indeed the young cooks create a cheerful atmosphere. Puzzle-solving is for evenings only; lunch is traditional kaiseki, finishing with sea bream rice with green tea poured over it.

Name: Shunka Nakamura
Description: Relentless curiosity is the driving force of this chef. After going to Hong Kong to study Cantonese cuisine, he then worked at a kappo to learn about Japanese food. He calls the marriage of these two shunka, which roughly translates as ‘Chinese food with a seasonal sensibility’. Spring rolls of pike conger or conger eel are one example. The steamed chicken is a secret recipe passed on from his Hong Kong mentor. He presents the home-cooked flavours that Hongkongers love.

Name: Nœud. TOKYO
FacilitiesAndServices: Air conditioning,Counter dining,Restaurant offering vegetarian menus
Description: The focus of the cuisine is aroma above all. Dishes are built around vegetables, with parts such as leaves, stalks and peels transformed through a variety of cooking methods. Presentation is modern, a layering of flavours and textures. The restaurant’s approach of ‘All Sustainable French’, using everything, wasting nothing, is its way of discovering new facets of familiar ingredients. Recycled materials in the décor reflect the same conviction.

Name: Lyla
Description: Like the restaurant’s name, the cuisine is born of the sensibility of poetry, a work of modern art. Meals begin with contemporary appetisers before proceeding to classic fare. In the presentation, great attention is paid to crockery shapes and colours. Sauces for fish and meat dishes are prepared with wine pairings in mind; flavours are calculated to impart a certain sourness. The infused fruit juice sourced from Oita proclaim the chef’s birthplace.

Name: Akasaka Watanabe
Description: Dressed in white and sporting a bow tie, Yujiro Watanabe greets his guests with a smile. His spirit of graceful service is ‘delicious, fun and welcoming’. Sesame ground in a large bowl, karasumi (salted and dried grey mullet roe) shaved before customers’ eyes and the staging of the kitchen are three shared moments. Rice from Niigata, produced by his sister and her husband, is used. Sea bream chazuke (green tea poured over rice) is a legacy from his mentor. The gratitude is palpable, the conversation lively.

Name: caillou
Description: The carefully selected fare borrows ideas from the local markets of France. The style here is to confer with the chef before you order, perusing the showcase full of ingredients in front of the kitchen. Simple French items dominate, such as smoked salmon, pâté en croûte, fish du jour, pig’s feet, cured beef and vanilla ice cream. Pointing and choosing adds to the fun, and dishes are prepared in the quantity you prefer.

Name: IL GiOTTO
Description: In this white-walled detached house facing Komazawa-Koen Avenue, with its cosy, wood-lined interior, sounds of food preparation from the open kitchen, and the atmosphere of a shop run by a couple, guests feel invited into a home. Chef Naofumi Takahashi specializes in meat dishes, such as bruschetta with home-cured ham and simmered tripe. He takes special pride in his slow-aged, char-grilled meats. Beef, aged to enhance umami, is seasoned with salt and pepper.

Name: sio AOYAMA
Description: The Aoyama branch of sio fairly bubbles with imaginative power. The foundation is French, but the direction is creative, paying no attention to genre. Meats are grilled over a wood fire to draw out the full strength of their inherent flavours. If you sit at the counter, you can gaze into the flickering flames and enjoy the aroma of meat sizzling on the grill. The restaurant’s name, ‘sio’, is Japanese for ‘salt’, affirming the importance of this vital seasoning. The restaurant prides itself on salting with just the right touch to highlight flavours.

Name: Fugu Club miyawaki Bettei
Description: Takashi Miyawaki is taking fugu (blowfish) cuisine to a new level. Thick-cut sashimi is dressed with caviar and olive oil; skin and milt become spring rolls. While the fare is strictly Japanese, Western ingredients and oils are added to good effect. Even pots of stew are served individually, for a special twist. Prices are set quite reasonably to ensure people see fugu as accessible. Now a much-loved dish especially on celebratory occasions, fugu brings happiness through eating.
